CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 4th DECEMBER, I860. The Mails from Europe arrived here ou Monday morning. The Stine arrived at St. Thomas on Saturday. The London Journals are devoid of much political news. Garibaldi has retired from public life for the present, after having resigned his Dietatorship into the hands of the King of Sardinia. He advises the preparation of a large army, as he supposes war to be inevitable next year. The news of the surrender of Gaeta is daily expected, as the representatives of Russia, Prussia, Austria and Spain have advised Francis the Second | to leave the country. The news from China, which will be found in another part of our columns, points to a speedy conclusion of peace. The þÿ þÿDagblad states that Secretary C. Hattensen has on the 30th Oct., received His þÿMajesty s appointment to the office which he now fills.

ITALY, THE TWO SICILIES Garibaldi having conquered a kingdom makes a present of it to Victor Emmanuel, and withdraws to bis little island of Caprera. On the morning of Thursday week Garibaldi, aeconr panied by the Ministry, formally presented to the King the result of the þÿ plebiscite. Ilis Majesty received them in the Throne Room. The Minister Signor Conforti addressed the King thus: þÿ þÿ Sire, þÿ The Neapolitan people, assembled in their electoral þÿ comitia, have proclaimed you King by an immense majority. Nine millions of Italians are uniting themselves jo the other provinces which your Majesty governs with so much wisdom, verifying your solemn promise that Italy should belong to the Italians þÿ The King replied in a few expressive words. The deed of annexation was then drawn up, the Dictatorship ceased, and the Ministry resigned. The enthusiasm of the people continues. The ex- Dictator, in his farewell proclamation,, tells his companions in arms to be ready to follow him again, as it is likely that a fresh conflict will break out in Italy in March, 1861. Garibaldi says that one million of men and arms will be wanted. Garibaldi took leave of his Majesty yesterday week, overwhelmed with the most striking demonstrations of sympathy from the King, his staff officers, and the army in general. King Victor Emmanuel has published the following proclamation : þÿ TO THE NEAPOLITAN AND SICILIAN PEOPLE. Universal suffrage gives me the sovereign | power over those noble provinces. I accept

this solemn decree of tbe national will, not from any ambition to reign, but from the consciousness of being an Italian My duties increase with those of all Italians'. More than ever a serious accord and a constant abnegation have become necessary. All parties must how with devotedness before the majesty of Italy, which God has rescued. II, re we must establish a Government guaranteeing a life of freedom to the people, and strict honesty of purpose in the face of public opinion I rely upon the efficacious co-operation of all honest men. Wherever the law imposes a curb on power and secures liberty, the Government can do as much for the public good ns tho people for virtue. We nm>t prove to Europe that, if the irresistible force of events has conquered the treaties established for the secular thraldom of Italy, we know how to restore among the united nation the empire j of those immutable principles without which every nation is diseased, and every authority meeting with opposition is unstable. Victor Emmanuel. The Turin Cabinet are actively proceeding to the reorganisation of the Government of tho Two Sicilies. Farini for Naples, and Monte- Zemolo for Sicily, are to be not. Royal Commissioners, but Govcrnors-General of their respective kingdoms. Till the convocation of the great Italian Parliament, in January they will exercise full dictatorial powers, doing as they please both as to laws, institutions, and persons. Cordova goes out. as Minister for the Finances in Sicily; La Farina as Home Minister anti

Minister of Public Security, or of tho Police. Father Lanza is appointed Minister of Public Instruction. Whilst Victor Emmanuel, by the force of arms and by the free choice of the people, reigns over the Two Sicilies, the King (rather the ex-KingJ thereof, Franeis II., still holds

out at Gaeta. By the latest accounts wo learn that he obstinately repudiates all advice to give up the contest, and relying upon General Bosco, who.-e parole expired on Tuesday, and an army of 10,000 men which lie yet has, means to prolojg a hopeless resistance. It is moreover said that a þÿ1 russianGeneral has arrived at Gaeta on a mission A Portuguese aud two Spanish frigates have arrived off Gaeta. j

THE WAR IN þÿCHINA. THE ADVANCE UPONPEKIN The negotiations at Tiou-Tsin furnish another chapter in the history of Chinese deception. The London Gazette of Tuesday Dight publishes an important despatch from Loid Elgin, communicating the grounds upon which he broke off the negotiations with the Chinese Commissioners. It appears that his Lordship instructed his secretaries, Messrs. Wade and Parkes, to wait upon the Imperial Commissioners with a draught of the convention, upon the signing of which Lord Elgin had promised that hostilities should cea.-e. The artiule agreeing to pay an indemnity of eight millions of taels appeared to occasion the Commissioners great difficulty ; and ultimately they stated that they could not sign the treaty without first referring it to the Emperor. Lord Elgin regarded this as a breach of faith on their part, nud accuses them of having assumed the title of Plenipotentiaries when they were not invested with full powers. They requested

Lord Elgin to þÿ wait three days or so at Tien- Tsin, so as fo enable everything to be settled þÿsatisfactorily. Lord Elgin regarded this þÿ as a deliberate desigu to create delay, which might throw us into the þÿwinter. Upon this he gave instructions to Sir Hope Grant to advance to Tung-Chow, where negotiations may possibly have been resumed, adding that be could not resume negotiations until he had reached that place. The Times nud Daily Nexus publish long and interesting letters from their special correspondents. The rupture of negotiations took place on the 7th and on the 8th the army moved forward on Pekin. On the 9th Lord Elgin followed, and ou the lltli the outposts of the allied force had reached a place called Yung- Tsun, forty-five miles tioni Pekin. Writing from that place on the ll'li of September, the Times correspondent says : þÿ þÿ We reached this place yesterday, after two þÿdays march through frequent villages, and over a flat alluvial plain eoveied with millet. Had we to contend with an enterprising enemy this march would have been attended with the greatest difficulties. In the first three miles out of Tien- Tsin we crossed seven bridges over wide canals, not Oita of which had been broken. The road theuce ruus along the south bank of the river, and a few jingal-meu in the high millet on the opposite side might have galled us fearfully. Had barricades been made, or the roads been broken up in the villages, a serious obstacle would have been afforded; for the streets are

narrow, and every inch of country, save ODly where the road is made or houses arc built, is covered with millet fourteen feet high. But the þÿ enemy is iu visible, and, according to the þÿvillagers account, the Tartars were too much alarmed in their flight to think of anything l except their own safety. Soon after encamping hero yesterdav we had a tremendous thunderstorm. For seven hours the rain descended in torrents, and soon converted the country into a swamp. The road was quite impracticable for artillery, and the order was given that we should not march this tuorniug. However, it cleared up at eleven p.m., and now the sun has risen with every promise of fine weather, and a fresh breeze is blowing that will soon diy the roads. þÿ flag A of truce has just come in, borne by two mandarins of the fourth class. They aunouuco that the leading member of the war party, Tsai-wau, President of the Imperial Court of PunislnueDt, and Mu-liyn, President of the Coun cil of War, and a member of the clique which has of late directed the Government, are coming down to Ticn-Tsin in order to treat. The order is given t hat we march at noon, which is the best answer to this announcement. Tsai-wan and Mu-liyr will be met on the line of march and informed that the Ambassadors refuse to treat before arriving at Tung-Chow. At last the fox is unearthed, and it will he our own fault if ho be not killed in the open. The Pekinese will sca European force under the walls of their capital, and the leaders of the war party, unable to proo

tect them, suing for mercy. Last night, during the storm, the drivers of the carts hired at Ticn- Tsiu bolted with their horses. This was, no doubt done by order of the Government, in hopes of delaying our march. The scheme will not succeed. A number of junks have been seized and manned by sailors, and, as the river runs up to Tung-Chow, the baggage will be carried by water instead of by þÿlaud. ITALIAN POLICY OF GREAT BRITAIN. The following di-patch has been addressed to the British Minister at Turin: þÿ Foreign-Office, Oct. 27. Sir, þÿ It appears that the late proceedings of the King of Sardinia have been strongly disapproved of by several of the principal Courts of Europe. The Emperor of the French, on hearing of the invasion of the Papal States by the aimy ot General Gialdim, withdrew his Minister from Turin, expressing at the same time the opinion of the Imperial Government in condemnation of the invasion of the Roman territory. I he Emstrong terms his iudignatiun peror of Russia has. we are told, declared ot at the entrance in the army of the King of Sardinia into the Neapolitan territory, mission from Turin. The Prince Regent ol Prussia has also thought it necessary to couvey to Sardinia a sense of his displeasure, hut he lias not thought it necessary to remove the Prussian Minister from Turin. After these diplomatic acts it would scarcely be just to Italy, or respectful to the other Great Powers of littrope, were the Government ot her Maj esty any longer to withhold the expression of their opinion. In so doing, however, her þÿMajesty s Government have no intention raise a dispute upon the reasons which have to been given in the name of the King of Sardinia for the invasion of the Roman and Neapolitan States. Whether or uo the Pope was justified in defending his authority by means ot foreign beat Mr. L. þÿWood s levies, whether the King ot the 1 wo Sicilies, while still maintaining his flag at Capua and

Gaeta, can be said to have abdicated, are not the arguments upon which her þÿMajesty Go- s vernment propose to dilate. The large questions which appear to them to be at issue are these: þÿ Were the people of Italy justified in asking the assistance ot the King of Sardinia to relieve ments with which they were discontented ? them Irom Govern- þÿ and was the King of Sardinia justified in furnishing the assistance of his arms to the people of the Roman and Neapolitan States ? There appear to have been two motives which have induced the people of the Roman and Neapolitan States to join willingly in the subversion of their Governments. The first of these was that the Government of the Pope and the King of the Two Sicilies provided so ill for the administra- J. þÿMc In- tion of justice, the protection of personal liberty, and the general welfare of their people, that their subjects looked forward to the overthrow of their rulers as a necessary preliminary to all improvement in their condition. The second motive was, that a conviction had spread since the year 1849 that the only manner in which Italians could secure their independence Government one strong of foreign control was by forming for the whole of Italy. The struggle of Charles Albert, in 1848, and the sympathy which the present King of Sardinia has shown for the Italian cause have naturally caused the association of the name of Victor Emmanuel with the single authority under which the Italians aspire to live. Looking at the question in this view, her

þÿMajesty s Government must admit that their Italians themselves are the best judges of the own interests. That eminent jurist Vattel, when discussing the lawfulness of the assistance given by tho United Provinces to the Prince of Grange, when he invaded England and overturned the throne of James II., says, þÿ The authority of the Prince of Orange had, doubtless, an influence on the deliberations of the States-General, but it did not lead them to tho commission of au act of injustice; for when a people, for good roasons,

take up arms against an oppressor, it is hut an act of justice and generosity to assist brave meu in the defence of their þÿliberties. Therefore, according to Vattel, the question resolves itself into this þÿ Did the people of Naples and of the Roman States take up arms against their Governments for good reasons? Upon this grave matter her þÿMajesty Go- s vernment hold that the people in question are themselves the best judges of their own affairs. Her þÿMajesty Government s do not feel justified in declaring that the people of Southern Italy had not good reasons for throwing oft their allegiance to their former Governments; her Majesty's Government cannnt, therefore, pretend to blame the King of Sardinia for assisting them. There remains, however, a question of fact. It is asserted by the partisans of the fallen Governments that the p ople of the R nnan States were attached to the Pope, and the people of tho kingdom of Naples to the dynasty of Francis 11., but that Sardinian agents and foreign adventurers have, by force and intrigue, subverted the thrones of those Sovereigns. It is difficult, however, to believe, after tho astonishing events which we have seen, that the Pope and the King of the Two Sicilies possessed the love of their people. How was it, one must ask, that the Pope found it impossible to levy a Roman army, and that he was forced to rely' almost entirely upon foreign mercenaries? How did it happen, again, that Garibaldi conuud has withdrawn his eutire j quered nearly all Sicily with 2000 men, and

marched from Reggio to Naples with 5000 ? How but from the universal disaffection of the people of the Two Sicilies? Neither can it bo said that this testimony of the popular will was capricious or causeless. þÿF orty years ago the Neapolitan people made an attempt regularly and temperately to reform their Government under the reigning dynasty. The Powers of Europe, assembled at Laybach, resolved, with the exception of England, to put down this attempt by force. It was put down, and a large foreign army was left in the Two Sicilies to maintain social order. In 1848 the Neapolitan people again attempted tosecureliberty under the Bourbon dynasty ; but their best patriots atoned by an imprisonment of ten years for the offence of endeavouring to free their country ; what wonder, then, that in 1860 theNeapolitans, mistrustful and resentful, should throw off the Bourbons, as in 1688 England had thrown off the Stuarts ? It must be admitted undoubtedly that the severance of the tics which bind together a Sovereign and his subjects is in itself a misfortune. Notions of allegiance become confused, the succession of the throne is disputed, adverse parties threaten the peace of society ; rightB and pretensions are opposed to each other, and mar tho harmony of the State. Yet it must be acknowledged, on the other hand, that the Italian revolution has been conducted with sittgular temper and forbearance. The subversion of existing power has not been followed, as is too often

the case, by au outbreak of popular vengeance. The extreme views of democrats have nowhere prevailed. Public opiuion has checked the excesses of the public triumph. The venerated forms of constitutional monarchy have been associated with the name of a Prince who represents an ancieut and glorious dynasty. Such having been the causes and the concomitant circumstances of the revolution of Italy , her þÿMajesty Government s cau see no sufficient ground for the severe censure with which Austria, þÿF rance, Prussia and Russia have visited the acts of the King of Sardinia. Her þÿMajesty s Government will turn their eyes rather to the gratifying prospect of a people building up the edifice of their liberties, and consolidating the work of their independence amid the sympathies and good wishes of Europe. þÿ I have, Ac., (Signed) J. Scientific readers are aware that the undulatory theory of light, though pretty generally accepted, is nevertheless on its trial, and liable
to modification, as new facts are discovered.

The question is one of first-rate importance, in a scientific point of view, and rarely admits of the popular illustration; but in a paper read Mr. Manchester Philosophical Society by before J. Smith, we find an account of a lew interesting experiments, which may be repeated without the use of recondite appliances, and which appeal in a striking manner to the eye. Mr. Smith holds that the vibrations of the luminous ether are not such as science teaches, and that we may dispense with the notion that rays are of different refrangibility. He assumes that white light is the motion of an ether, while blackness is the state of no motion, and shews that certain colours þÿ blue, red, or yellow þÿ are producible by the alternate action of light and shadow þÿ taking shadow to signify blackness. Cause a paralleloof white card-board to revolve over a black surface with the same rapidity as the vibrations of light, and the colour will appear to be blue or | purple, according to circumstances. A disk ground, painted with black concentric riugs, when becomes completely coloured on a white swiftly whirled ; the black and white disappear, and on a bright cloudy day the disk shews a light yellowish green, two different shades of purple and a pink. We take from the St. Croix Avis a small article referring to the adverse winds that recently prevailed and retarded We between that Island and this. all intercourse believe the packet-schooner with the Mails to meet the Atrato for Europe was four days coining over, and consequently failed to reach here in time, so that those Mails did net go lorward in that instance. The Avis views it as a favorable occasion to point to the necessity of having a steamer placed between tho two Islands. We say by all means. Let the Government augment its subsidy for carrying the Mails and other services between the two places, and the inducement would be sufficient to encourage a Company to be formed and a steamer purchased. We have now lying in our port a þÿvessel the Princeþÿ that would exactly suit, so that really there would he no need to go very far in search of one. It only wants action and liberality on

S T.. C R 0 : X A V ; s, the part of the Government and we could inaugurate the new year with the acquisition of a steam communication between the sister Islands. It is believed that, such communication would not be in operation three months before the travel between the two places would increase four-fold. ( From the London Evening Mail.) The Swedish Government has just taken a step in advance of all other Continental Powers. It has decreed the abolition of the Passport System. Though the state of Europe is not 1 particularly encouraging, and though wars and rumours of wars might have furnished more \ timid rulers with pretexts for delay, the Govern ment of Sweden has struck boldly at the nuisauce. It. has not done the good work negligently or with reserve. The entire system, with all its complicated abominations and follies, is swept away at once, and it is openly proclaimed that anybody may henceforth enter the Swedish territory, traverse, or leave it with as little hindrance or affront as would be encountered in our own country. Such atr act. deserves all praise, and we can only hope, for the sake of civilization, that so good an example may speedily find imitators. We are aware that in some of the German States common sense has proved i too strong for law, and that the system, though not formally abolished, has been allowed to drop gradually into disuse, but Sweden, we believe, is the first of the coutineutal kingdoms which J has beeu enlightened enough to rt pudiate this mechanism of mischief by a public edict, and declare that as far as her territories are concerned every one shall be free to come and free to go. All Europe has been talking of late years about Free Trade, but it is evident that Free Trade requires freedom of locomotion. Free Trade means free transit, and there is no transit more important than that of men themselves. A

passport system amounts, in point of fact, to a duty levied upon men instead of goods, and exacted in the most inconvenient coiu. A moneytax paid once for all as the price of free travelling would be far more endurable than the sys- ; tem actually maintained. It would be a highly impolitic tax no doubt, and would probably scandalize the very statesmen who uphold a system infinitely worse. No French or Austrian Minister would like to recommend that every foreign merchant or visitor should be stopped at the frontier of the State and fined heavily for his | intention of entering the kingdom. The scheme would seem positively outrageous, and yet it would do much less harm than the practice now prevailing. It would add but a trifling charge to the expenses of travelling, and it would exempt the travellers from all delay and annoyance afterwards. As it is, no one can tell when he is safe, aud the pecuniary fine is paid without any privilege to correspond. It is useless to say that Passports are þÿ þÿgratuitously furnished when they can only be obtained at such a cost of time and trouble as is far more vexatious than any money charge. A traveller on the Continent had far better pay his commissionaire at once than exhaust his patience and waste bis day in hanging about the purlieus of a Passportoffice. This is understood on all sides; but the nuisance is that the payment does no good, and that the Passport-bearer is still liable to be stopped and questioned at every barrier exactly as if

he had paid nothing at all. The absurdity of the system is brought out into strong relief by the fact, of which most travellers are cognizant, that the machinery for the most part is utterly useless even from the point of view which its own advocates would select. If the Passport System means anything, it must mean that every traveller is to !> identified by his Passport at every town which he visits, just as a bale of goods is examined at every barrier maintained for the purposes of þÿCustoms duties. But everybody who has travelled knows full well that he may very likely roam about for months together þÿ of-leave, indeed, we have occasionally heard without being once asked for his ticketthis chance alleged in exculpation of the system. Men will sometimes observe that they have travelled a good deal, and yet were never required to produce their Passport from first to last. They forget, however, that they for required to procure it, to pay it. to carry were invariably it about their persons, and to have it always forthcoming at a þÿmoment notice s under penalty of most serious inconvenience þÿ extending, perhaps, even to imprisonment. It is as much ns if a man were to remark after travelling through the Desert or the Campagna, that, though, he was, indeed, obliged to carry a couple of revolvers at, bis belt, and to sleep with a sword under his

Ss þÿT Us $ ft (I AVIS l , pillow, he was never once molested. What creates the trouble in these cases is the known risk and the ever present liability, agaiust which it is continually requisite to guard. It is possible enough that you may never be asked lor your Passport from the time that you set foot on French or Belgian ground to the moment that you prepare to quit it. It is certain, however, that you are liable to be asked for it at any hour of any day, and that if it happens to be missing, or defective, or irregularly drawn, yon may find yourself in the position of a captured deserter or a returned convict. This is where the shoe pinches, and to say that the annoyance actually happens only to one man out of twenty is simply to show that the system has no real use If it were a reality, all men would be questioned alike, yust as all ships alike are examined by Custom-house officeis. As it is, though the actual evil may but rarely occur, the contingency is always imminent. When a pestilence is raging not one man in a thousand will probably be carried off, but all the thousand share the apprehension and the peril. We need hardly advert to the well-known fact that all this machinery is found of no avail whatever against the particular class of characters most obnoxious to the promoters of the system. Any conspirator, revolutionist, or demagogue can traverse with perfect security any country, however jealously guarded, which he is desirous of visiting, and the reason is plain. A Passport though an insufferable nuisance to an iuuoceut

traveller, is a godsend to the political adventurer. It supplies him with the very thing that he wants þÿ a character. Without his passport he might be at some loss to give an account of himself, but in that document everything is done for him, aud all the trouble taken off his hands. If the police approach with any awkward inquiiies he produces the precious iustrumeut, which is as good as an affidavit. There he appears set down, and described from head to foot, and is, moreover, particularly recommended to the authorities lor aid aud succoui in case of need. Supposing the document to be irreproachably correct þÿ which, of course, is invariably the case in all such instances þÿ the police are at fault. They can do nothing with their man. They may dislike his looks, or distrust his purpose, but they are powerless iu the matter, for they have fixed their own terms lor travelling, and he has complied with them. They have chosen to treat locomotion itself as a suspicious proceeding which must be formally accounted for. They require that every traveller shall carry with him is aim produce on demand a certificate that he of respectable c haracter, and not a rogue, ftlou, filibuster, or firebrand. The man before them lias accepted these conditions, and is prepared with precisely the certificate for which they stipulate. There is the documeut þÿ sworn, stamped, aud attested before all the proper authorities. Not a flaw nor a crevice can be found in the testimonial from beginning to end. Nobody can

pick a hole in such a comprehensive warranty, aud it passes current accordingly. A passport took Orsini aud his accomplices into the heart of Paris, aud protected him thereuntil he ventured on his nefarious attempt. Such people never blunder and never suffer. The victims are the innocent visitors iu search of recreation or instruction, who, knowiug no harm and thinking no evil, overlook some little formality, aud tumble headhong into the police trap However, there seems a better time comiDg. Sweden has led the way gallantly, and within the last few weeks even absolute Russia has modified the regulations of her Passport System. Free Italy is not likely to lag behind iu such a race, and perhaps before long we shall see Europe relieved of a system which has done more mischief than any other species of restriction. There is no commerce which it is more desirable to encourage tbau that between men and men; no custom more pernicious than that which by confining people to the place of their birth deprives them of the liberality of fueling which intercourse with their fellow-creatures would create. If war is ever to be made impossible by the mutual acquaintance and esteem of nations, the good work must be commenced by the abolition of a system which treats every man as a criminal on his defence as soon as he sets foot in any country but his owd.

Scene in an Australian Theatre. þÿ "The curtain rose. A French dancer þÿ an elegant, supple young lady, of no great beauty, but much expression, and apparently on very good terms with herself þÿ appeared in the scene in her short lace dress, received by an outburst of applause and by the martial trumpets of the orchestra. But from the other side came a youthful, blooming Spanish creole, with beautiful eyes, large and soft; her complexion rosy, her figure tall þÿ in fact, the impersonation of Terpsichore. She bowed modestly þÿ it was her first appearance at Melbourne þÿ and the enthusiasm of the public, surprised by her beauty, manifested itself in vehement cheers. The two dancers struggled for the palm of vietory in a graceful tarantula. Like two glittering butterflies, they whirled round, accompanied by music and applause. The mercurial Parisienne made use of her most seductive viles, of her most refitted 'pirouettes,' of her most enchanting attitudes; but the creole seemed patronized by t he Graces themselves. Thundering applause encouraged her, and, as often as she came forward with her graceful modesty, nosegays, rings and bracelets were thrown at her feet. The French lady struggled with her last strength against the triumph of her rival, until, disheartened and exhausted, she fell to the ground. The creole approached her with compassion to raise Iter, when suddenly the Parisienne darted up, and, with looks of hatred and fury, boxed the ears of her rival. The audience hissed and hoot-

ed, while she exclaimed with much passion, 'The wretch tripped me!' The poor creole declared with dignity that she was innocent of the meanness; but a vulgar word which slipped out of the lips of the French dancer against her suddenly aroused all the passions of the South in her bosotn, and a singular struggle began. The two excited ladies rushed upon each other, and wrestled and tore, and pulled one another's hair, while the thunders ol the gallery made the whole atmosphere vibrate. I never saw a more natural performance. The better class of the public did not interfere, hut seemed rather to be amused by these Olympic exercises, until the creole, bleeding and fainting, was carried away from the scene. Some officers who from a box had witnessed the spectacle were revolted at the conduct of the Parisienne, and sent for the police to arrest her, but her frieuds collected and resisted the constables. A riot ensued; a portion of the public rushed on tho stage; they jumped across the orchestra; the fiddles and bass-viols were broken; the ladies were fainting; children crying ; and I took to my heels with my fiddle, and ran away without slopping until T reached my hotel." þÿ Liverpool Mercury.

From the London Times, December. 1. There is a story of a young English ensign whose nerve failed him the first time that he found himself under fire, till he was recalled to his duty hy the kind hut stern remonstrances of an old Scotch sergeant. The plunge once taken, the youth's blood began to warm, and before long he was recklessly exposing himself in the thickest of the light, when wary he felt his arm grasped by the same old soldier, with the words' " Re- " member your niither, lad þÿ remember " your mither !" INo one would have believed, while the present King of Gaeta was still King of Naples, hesitating and trembling at the very name of Garibaldi, that lie would ever show spirit and obstinacy enough to justify the moral ofour story. It was said that he would lose his kingdom, like Louis XVI. and Louis Philippe, for want of the pluck to show himself on horseback at the head of histroops. Strange rumours were afloat of his fatuous indifference to the progress of events þÿ an indifference which, in his position, could only be attributed to imbecility or cowardice. It is but fair to confess that the Ki ng's subsequent cond ct has, in some degree, belied his reputation. If he has given no proof of strategical or administrative capacity, and has alienated some waverers by his impolitic implacability, he has shown that he can stand at bay manfully, and has the respectable quality of not knowing when lie is beaten. He has .exhibited, "for a Bourbon," considerable virtues, lie has shown more regard for the personal convenience and

safety of others than for his own ; his has sent away, not only his stud and he jewels, hut bis mother, his wife, and his children ; he has advised those Ambassadors who still stood by him to retire to pect of a bombardment. This is dy- Home ; yet he himself awaits the pros- " ing game," and commands a sort of respect, even when it fails to command sympathy. As between Francis and Victor Emmanuel, there is not a word to be said against the lawfulness of such tactics. No European despot can be expected to emulate the magnanimity of the Roman Emperor Otlio when he saw that all was lost, or to resort to the Japanese expedient of disembowelling himself in the presence of an inevitable calamity. So long as there his remained or hint any chance of saving crown, to even of inflicting any substantial injury on his enemy, it was venial enough to struggle for existence. What we submit to those, if there be any, who are still Bourbonists at heart is that this chance is now exhausted, and that common humanity demands the termination of a contest which can have but one issue. However little weight may be attached to historical parallels as lessons of policy, it is impossible not to be struck by the similarity of the circumstances attending the present Neapolitan revolution and those of the Belgian revolution in1830. In that case, as in this, a popular insurrection had wrested several fine provinces from a dynasty equally odious to the people, though it had not laid the foundations of its unpopularity so deep-

ly or so durably. Long after the inexorable logic of facts had pronounced the exclusion of the House of Orange ; after blunders, and intrigues, and futile Republican demonstrations enough to disgust all the friends of liberty had ended in the election of a Constitutional Prince ; and after the Great Powers of Europe

$5 Tj' $ d ll & had recognized the separation of Belgium from Holland, the King of Holland still insisted on General Cliasse holding the citadel of Antwerp for himself. Belgian independence had been proclaimed at Brussels in November, 1 830, but it was not till the '24th of December, 1832, when it had been bombarded for nearly a month, that the citadel of Antwerp surrendered, and even then " the King of Holland, with ehar- "acteristic obstinacy, refused to ratify " the let ins of the capitulation." So far the parallel holds, and we shall be very much surprised if Francis II. gives up the last rag of his power with a better grace than the Prince of Orange. But there is one point where the analogy notably fails, and that is the attitude assumed by France towards the contending Powers. France was then governed by a King who owed his title to a revolution of which that in Belgium c was an offshoot, and Louis Philippe deter mined to hasten the inevitable event of the contest by compulsory measures. It may be difficult to reconcile the proceedings of the French Government, to which our own was a party, with the doctrines of non-intervention, but it is certain that much bloodshed was spared and a peaceful settlement facilitated by the act of France in casting the weight of her sword into the scale. It is somewhat unfortunate that at the present crisis, when bare neutrality was all that was required, she should have contributed by an arbitrary interference of a totally different kind to prolong a state of

things mischievous to the interests of Italy. We cannot tell whether this course is to be attributed to mere indecision on the Emperor's part or to some dark and hitherto occult motive þÿ whether he is waiting for what used to be called in 1848 ",new developments," or whether his object is only to break the fall of a tottering dynasty ; but we cannot doubt that he is responsible for the chief hitch in the solution of the Italian question. If F rancis II. wishes to be able to say that, like Francis L, he has "lost all except honour," lie has already done more than enough. There is a point in many a losing match when the game ceases to be worth the candles. A lawyer does not provoke a crushing decision after repeated intimations truni the (Jourt that he has "no case." A chess-player does not go on obstinately exchanging pawn after pawn when he has iosl all Ins principal pieces; and a moment may come when the stanchest second will "throw up the sponge." There are other interests to lie considered besides those of the rival Kings þÿ the interests of the peaceful inhabitants of the Two Sicilies, and of the brave men who will not desert even a Bourbon Monarch in misfortune. We can hardly expect that a Prince who was prepared to turn the guns of St. Elmo against his own capital will have much consideration tor the former; but he may well hesitate before he sacrifices the citizens of Gaeta and the 20,001) troops who still defend the place to a mistaken point of honour. James II. was touched with a feeling of

remorse when he saw his old soldiers cut up by foreign troopers, but Francis has in his sole keeping the lives of men whose loyally has been tried to the utmost and has not been found wanting. He litis lavished grand crosses and broad ribands on foreign Ministers, and taken measures for their security, but he would earn a far more genuine gratitude by releasing from their allegiance the faith-

ful remnant of his followers. It is not his fault that lie is the victim of just vengeance, treasured up through many generations against his name and family. Let him accept this as his fate þÿ a fate which he inherited from a ler and worse men than himself; and, if he seeks materials for vindictive gratification, he will find them, as he watches the destinies of Italy from an Austrian or Spanish palace, in the struggles and humiliations through which a nation long demoralized by misrule must necessarily pass before it can prove itself truly worthy of freedom.

(be United States was read in Congress on the 4th ulto This important document, the last and the best from Mr. Buchanan, as it has been characterized in the United States, has been viewed in many lights by the American Press It hat, it is said, not satisfied the South nor pleased the North. It does not view the election of Mr. Lincoln as any provocation- for disunion ; nor does it consider that the South is in auy immediate danger of Northern aggres sion VVe have made a lew extracts from the Message, which, in its entirety, could uevev bo published in our columns.

The President, in relation to secession, recommends : " What in the meantime is tie responsibility and tiue position of the Executive? He is bouud by solemn oaths before God and tie country to take care that the laws be faithfully executed, and from this obligation he cannot be absolved by any human power. But what, if this performance of this duty, in whole or in part, has been rendered impracticable try events over which lie could have exercised no control ? Such at the present moment, is the case throughout the State of South Carolina, so far as the laws of tlie United States to secure the administration of justice by means of the Federal Judiciary are concerned. All the Federal officers within the limits through whose agency alone those laws can be carried into execution have already resigned We no longer have a District Judge, a Di-trict Attorney, or a Marshal in South Carolina, lu tact, the whole machinery of the Federal Governor nt, necessary for t ho distribution of remedial justice among the people, has been demolished, and it would be difficult, if not impossible, to repl.n-e it. "1 should feel myself rt errant to my duty, were I not to express an opinion en this important subject. The question lairly stated is; lias the Constitution delegated to Congress the pow er to coerce a State in submission which is intending to withdraw, or lias actually withdrawn from the' Confederacy ? If answered in the affirmative, it must be on the principle that the

power lias beeu conferred upon Congress to declare and make war against a State. " After much serious reflection, I have arrived at the conclusion that no such power has been delegated to Congress, or to any other department of the Government. It is manifest upon inspection of the Constitution, that this is not among the specific or enumerated powers granted to Congress, and it is equally apparent that its exorcise is not necessary and proper for carrying into execution any odc of these powers So far from this power having been delegated to Congress it was expressly refused by the Convention which formed the Constitution. '' It appears, from the proceedings of that body, that on the 31st day ot May, A. D. 1787, the clause authorizing the execution of the force of the whole against a delinquent State came up for consideration. Mr. Madison opposed it iu a brief but powerful speech, from which I shall extract but a single sentence : He observed, the use of force against a State would look more like a declaration of war tban an iufliction of punishment, and would probably be considered by the party attacked as a dissolution of all previous compacts by which it might be bound.

SPAIN. Our relations with Spain are now of a more complicated though less dangerous character than they have been for many years. Our citizens have long held, and continue to hold, numerous claims against the Spanish Government. These had been ably urged tor a series of years I outrages upon by our successive diplomatic representatives at Madrid (hut without obtaining redress. The Spanish Gover inent finally agreed to institute a joiutcouimissiou for the adjustment of these claims, and on the 5th day of March, I860, coneluded a convention for the purpose, with our Minister at Madrid. Under this convention, what have been denominated " Cuban claims," amounting $128,635 to and 54 cents, in which moie than one hundred of out fellow-citizens are interested, were ree gnized, and the Spanish Government agreed to pay $100,000 of this amount ''within three months of the exchange of ratifications " The payment of the remaining $28,635 54 was to await the decision Commissioner for, > r against, " the Ami-tad of the claim j" but in any event t lie balance was to be paid to the claimants cither by Spain or the United Stati s. These teims I have every teason to know, are highly satisfactory to the holders of the Cuban claims. Indeed, they have made a formal offer authorizing the State Depat trnent to settle these claims, and to deduct the amount of the Amistad claim Iroin the sums which they are entitled to receive from Spain. This offer, of course, cannot be accepted All other claims of citiz ns of the United

States against Spain, or of subjects of the Queen of Spaiu against the United States, iucludmg the "Amistad claim,'' were by this convention referred to a hoaidot commissioners in the usual form. Neither the validity of t lie Amistad claim nor of any other claim against either party, with the single exception of the Cuban claims, was r. cognized by the cntiveutb n Indcid, the Spanish government did not insist that the validity of the Ami, tad claim thould he thus rceognizi d, not withstanding its payment had been recommended to Congress by two of my predecessors as well as by myself, and au appropriation for that purpose had passed the Senate of I the the United States. Tlicy weie content that it should lie submiiti d to the hoard for examination and decision, like the other claims. Both governnii nts wcie hound respectively to pay the amounts awarded to the s, veral claimants "at. such times and places as may he fixed by and according to the tenor of said awards." 1 transmit!) d this convention to the Senate for llieir con»iitutio(ial action on the 3id of May, 1860, aud on the 2? li of the succeeding June they detei mined that they would "not advise and consent" to its ratification. Those proceedings place our relations with Spain in nn awkward and embarrassing position. It is more than probable that the final adjustment of these claims will devolve upon my successor. 1 reiterate the recommendation contained in my annual Message of December, 1858, and repeated in that ot I860, in lavor of the acquisi-

tion of Culm from Spain by fair purchase. I tinn y believe that such all acquisition would contribute essi ntially to the well luing and prosperity of both eountiies in all future time, as well as prove the ceituin means of immediately abolishing t e Afiiean slave trade throughout the world. 1 would not repeat this recommendation upon the present occasion, if I believed that t lie transfer of Cuba to the United States, upon conditions highly favorable to Spain, could justly tarnish the national honor of the proud and ancient Spanish monarchy. Surely no person ever attributed to the first Napoleon a disregard of the national honor of France, for transferring Louisiana to the United States tor a fair equivalent both in money and commercial adva ntnges. MEXICO. Our ii'lwtions with Mexico remains in a most unsatisfactory condition. In tny last two annual messages I discussed extensively the subject of these relations, and do not now propose to repeat at length the facts aud arguments then presented. They proved conclusively that our citizens re-iding in Mexico, and our merchants trading thereto, had suffered a series of wiotrgs and outrages such as we have never patiently homo from any other nation. For these our successive ministers, iuvoking the 1 these governments to deprive our neighboring

X\ & I0 u #«!;$ faith of treaties, had, in the name of their country, persistently demanded redress and j indemnification, but without the slightest effect. Indeed, so confident had the Mexican authorities become of our patient endurance, that they universally believed they might commit these Anierieau citizens with absolute impunity. Thus wrote our minister jn 1856, and expressed the opinion that "nothing hut a manifestation of the power of the Government, and of iis purpose to punish these wrongs will avail." Afterwards, in 8157, came the adoption of a new Constitution for Mexico, the election ot a President and Congress under its provision--, and the inauguration of the President. Within one short month, however, the Piesident was expelled from the capital by a rebellion in the army, and the supreme power of the Kepublie was a-signed to General Zaloaga. This usurper was in his turn soon compelled to retire and give place to General Miramon. Under the Constitution which had thus been adopted, Scnor Juarez, as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, became the lawful President of the Republic, and it was for the maintenance of the Constitution and his authority derived from it, that the civil war commenced, and still continues to be prosecuted. Throughout the year 1858 the constitutional party grew stronger and stronger. In the previous history of Mexico a successful military revolution at the capital had almost universally beeu the signal for submission throughout the Republic. Not so on the pres -nt occasion. A

majority of the citizens persistently sustained the constitutional government. When this was recognized, in April, 1850, by the Government of the Uiiited States, its authority extended over a large majority ol the Mexican States aud people, including Vera Cruz and all the other important seaports of the Republic. From that peiiod our commerce with Mexico begun to revive, and the constitutional government has afforded it all the protection in their power. Meanwhile the government of Miramon still held sway at the capital and over the surroundingjeountry, and continued its outrages against few American citizens who still had the courage to remain within its power. To cap the climax: After the battle of Tacubaya, in April, 1850, General Maiquez ordei el three citizens of the United States, two of them physicians, to he seized in the hospital at that place, taken out aud shot, without crime aud without trial. This was done, notwithstanding our unfortunate countrymen were at the moment eugaged in aff Tiling relief to the soldiers of both parties who had been wounded in the battle, without making any distinction between 1 them. The time had arrived, in my opinion, when this government was hound to exert its power to avenge and redress the wrongs of our citizens and afford them protection in Mexico. The interposing obstacle was that the poition of the country under the sway of Miramon could not ho reached without passing over territory under the jurisdiction of the constitutional government.

Under these circumstances I deemed it my duty to recommend to Congress, in tny last annual Message, the employment of a suffieieut military force to penetrate into (he interior, where the government of Miramon was to he found, with, or, il need he, without the consent of the Juarez government, though it was not doubted that . this consent could he obtaiued. Never have I had a clearer conviction on any subject than that of the justice as well as wisdom of such a policy. No other alternative was left, except the entire abandonment of our fellow citizens, who had gone to Mexico under the faith of treaties, to the systematic injustice, , cruelty and oppression of Miramon's government. Besides, it is almost certain tiiat the simple authority to employ this force would of itself have accomplished all our objects without striking a single blow. The constitutional government, would then ere this have been ready and willing, to the extent of its ability, to do us justice. In addition þÿ and I deem this a most important consideration-European governments would i have been deprived of all pretext to interfere in the territorial and domestic concerns of Mexico. We should thus have been relieved front the obligation of resisting even by force, should this become necessary, any attempt by

Republic of portions of her territory j a duty from which we could not shrink without abandoning the traditional and established policy of the American people. I am happy to observe j that, firmly relying upou the justice and good faith of these governments, there is no present danger that such a contingency will happen. Having discovered that my recommendations would not be sustained by Congress, the next alternative was to accomplish, in some degree, if p ossible, the same objects by treaty stipulations with the constitutional government. Such treaties were accordingly concluded by our late able and excellent Minister to Mexico, and on the 4th of January last were submitted to the Senate for ratification. As these have not yet received tire final action of that body, it would he improper lor me to present a detailed statement of their provisions. Still I may he permitted to express the opinion in advance that they arc calculated to promote the agricultural, manufacturing and ooinm rcial interests of tho country, and to secure our just influence with an adjoining republic as to whose lortunes and fate we can never feel indiffereut; whilst at the same time they provide for tho payment of a considerable amount towards the satisfaction of the claims of our injured Allow citizens. þÿ þÿ

THE LIBERTY OF THE PRESS From "The Press and the Public Service " By a Distinguished writer There most he either something very simple and loveable, or a vast deal of demure impudence, in the man who can fancy he has anything new to say about the Liberty of the Press in England. Nobody pretends to doubt it. Nodody pretends to dispute it. Any serious discussion on the subject seems like reviewing passages in our history which bear date nearly two hundred years ago. The most recent of the arguments on both sides tire as old as the time of Swift and Steele. An uninitiated person would he wholly unable to comprehend the utility of further speech or writing on the matter; for the curtest summary of the reasons which have been already used, is conclusive to all who can either learn or blush. It is doubtful, however, whether the true sttite of the case is very well understood ; whether any one can tell clearly how far the Liberty of the Press extends, how far it is a delusion, and how far a reality. Plain country gentlemen, and brave boys from college, honestly believe that every question as to the light and propriety of free political writing, has long been satisfactorily set at rest. Every student of constitutional law can tell glibly from Hallam and Itentham þÿ from the speeches of Fox and of Burke, of Erskine and of Macintosh, or from the living pages of Macaulay þÿ how the mischiefs which arise from a free Press may he easily and effectually obviated ; and that experience has repeatedly shown

British statesmen the peril and the utter fruitlessness of all attempts to curb it. A man must have thought little, or to little purpose, who is not in our days prepared to admit that any restriction which abridges the freedom of expression is a plain invasion of the rights and property of Englishmen. Restraints upon the Press serve but to enthral the judgment and conscience of the nation; to hind it over in slavery to tiny party tor the time in power; to condemn it to an unreasoning faith in one set of doctrines to-day, and in another set of doctrines to-morrow. They constitute, indeed, only a direct method to involve it in hopeless ignorance and error. Our title to the hard-won honour of a Press perfectly free is indeed so clear

anil indisputable, that it is strange we should not he allowed to enjoy it in peace. Its freedom was prepared by Bacon and Milton, by Halifax, Soniers, aud Locke. It was urged by the most eminent men among the founders of our constitution. The splendid rewards which were held out to slaves by the Stuarts, could bring no opponent of consequence into the field against it. At last it was conceded to us under William III.; and it is the greatest of the long list of benefits which the reign of that politic prince conferred upon us. Statesmen differing as widely as Bolingbroke and Hurley, as Walpole and the Grenvilles, as I'nt and Fox, as Canning and Sir It. Feel, have all acknowledged the inestimable value of that magnanimous concession. A list of the churchmen who have contrih ted to sanctify and secure it would comprise almost every divine remarkable for piety and learning during the last two centuries; Burnet and Atterhury, Butler and Warburton, Low ill, Watts, Kurd, Home, John Wesley, Nathaniel Lardner, with the respectable names of Bloomfield, Maltby, and Archbishop Whateley. Among the Lawyers who have defended it in times of danger will be found most of those who have been distinguished at the bar or on the bench. All the literary men of note have added to their reputation by asserting it. The obstinate contention, however, still goes on, the distressing strife between Power and Reason. The result, indeed, is always the same. Power is ultimately worsted in a cause which it

cannot avow without humiliation, and in which it cannot strike with safety. Still, it rarely gleans wisdom from the past; and none but the very highest order of statesmen can be brought to see the error and impolicy of engaging in a struggle where all is to he lost and nothing is to he gained; where victory, the heat of argument once over, would he more melancholy to a patriot than defeat. Every new generation is obliged to rescue the most precious of its privileges from the insidious encroachments of power, and to write in defence of the liberty which is the foundation of all other liberties; which is essential to everything that can with propriety be termed good government. Yet, if the freedom of the Press originally worked its way in this country, against numbers and prejudices ; it, in times of its infancy, the most bigoted and powerful oppressors could not prevail against it; surely when confirmed by time, and rooted in the affections of tiie people, it will be impossible to overthrow it. The attacks upon it which are sometimes made by good and conscientious men, must be classed with those weaknesses by which the greatest pay tribute to their mortality. Such a mistake, however, can only arise during the overwhelming pressure of public business, from the weariness of mind which is the penalty of overt bought, and oftasking the most generous nature too hardly. The Press is to us what the militia was to Charles I. If we were to lose all our other liberties, it would

ultimately bring the n all hack again. The liberty ofthe press, and the liberties of the country, must stand or la I f together. Other liberties have been held under governments; but the liberty of opinion keeps government itself in subjection to duty. It has therefore always been the last right that subjects have been able to wrest from power. When yielded, it has been yielded like a

s T« a o I i & y/ D banner to a foe, shred by shred, with tears and misgivings always ludicrously falsified in the sequel. Thus, the publication of debates in Parliament, seemed to the most liberal statesmen of the old school a practice full of danger; it is now regarded by the most prejudiced, as a safeguard of the constitution, tantamount to all the rest put together. It is certain, also, that the Press has become respectable, in proportion as it lias become free. Restrictions which suppressed truth and reason, made it licentious in the worst sense. When John Bunyan was in prison for expounding the Gospel to the poor, Wycherley was the most popular poet in England. When piety and virtue were gagged, iniquity and ribaldry were let loose. Now all may speak, no man offers an insult to religion or morality. Political liberty depends altogether upon the frequent and genuine manifestation of the public will. A free Press provides Parliament with the means of profiling by the information of the public. It enables electors to act with some knowledge of the conduct of their representatives. It informs legislators ot public opinion. It informs the people of the acts of legislation. It conduces to the maintenance of order; and prevents the stern necessity of revolutions. For nearly all that keeps up in us, permanently and effectually, the spirit of regard to liberty aud public good, we must look to the unshackled and independent energies of the Press. It is as the air which Liberty breathes ; it she

has it not, she dies. The Press virtually governs this country, because public opinion governs it, and is represented in no other way. For some months during the year it is the only check on the conduct of the Government and the power of the Crown. It is as important to a prime minister as to anybody else ; for, it it did not exist, he might lie replaced by his own lootman, without power of appeal or demur. When Parliament is sitting, it is only in the language of irony that it can be said to represent the nation. One man seals half a dozen members; another three or four þÿ all his dependants. Government lots great infiiience ; money has great influence; the Press is, therefore, the real representative of popular feeling þÿ the Parliament of the people. It has not been abused. It has made of Englishmen a race of earnest and thoughtful patriots, differing widely from the unruly populace of despotic states. So far is it from being true among us, that no stable government could exist with it, all admit that no good Government could exist without it. On the other hand, there is no freedom of the Press in Turkey þÿ no power to complain ; yet, of all countries, Turkey is that in which revolts arid revolutions are the most frequent and the most violent. A free Press is a real censorial power lodged in the impartial hands of the people. It gives them the right to express their disapprobation of public evils. It is a beneficent power, which begins where other checks fail ; it touches mat-

ter out of the reach ofthe law; it indicates, it does not punish ; it is the mildest, yet the most effectual, restraint that could be devised for authority. In all liberty there is, indeed, some danger; but so there is in all power. The question is, in which there is most danger, in power limited hy this check, or in power without this check to limit it. When complaints are freely heard and deeply considered ; when evils are spee-

dily reformed, then only is the utmost bound ot civil liberty attained, which wise men in our age and country are entitled to expect. The greater the number of temptations to which the exercise of political power is exposed, the more necessary is it to give to those who posses it the most powerful reasons for temperance and good conduct. There is no reason more forcible than is furnished by the consciousness of acting under the perpetual superintendence of the public. The public compose a tribunal which is more powerful than all other tribunals put together. An individual may pretend to disregard its decrees, þÿ to represent them as formed of fluctuating and opposite opinions, which destroy one another; hut every one feels, that though this tribunal may err, it is incorruptible; that it continually tends to become enlightened; that it unites all the wisdom and all the justice of the nation; that it always decides the reputation of public men ; and that the judgments it pronounces are inevitable. The enemies of publicity may be collected into three classes : the malefactor who seeks to escape the notice of the Judge; the tyrant who would stifle public opinion because he fears to hear its voice ; and the timid or indolent man, who complains of the general incapacity, in order to screen his own. Absolved from the beneficent censures of the Press, men in office, especially abroad, might dispense with being just, provided they were cautious not to infringe the letter of the law. But, hap-

pily, no man can now count upon secrecy; and irregularities are immediately divulged. Fortunately for England, the juryman knows that his verdict, the judge that his charge, will he laid before the public þÿ a public, keen discerning,, merciless to corruption. There is no man in office who does not feel compelled in almost every instance, to choose between his duty and the surrender of his reputation. Without publicity no good would be perm ment ; with it no evil can continue. A foreigner, who visited our policecourts, told Lord Mansfield he was surprised to find them so thinly attended by the public. "No matter, sir," replied the Chief Justice, shrewdly; "we sit every day in the newspapers." To say that an English judge is incorruptible is, therefore, scarcely to praise him. Public and free deliberations respecting the laws, measures, and conduct of official persons; also, are sure to operate in favour of the Government. If their position is rot utterly untenable, it enables them to refute objections, to confound false reports, to prove the necessity of the sacrifices required from the people. Government has always far greater means of employing the Press than are possessed by the Opposition. The Opposition must also assist them, even against its will ; for when they are in the right, who resists, strengthens. Finally, ministers are enabled to assure themselves ofthe success of a measure, before they risk their reputation upon it. by submitting it frankly to public

discussion; allowing it, prudently, to stand or fall hy its own merits ; or amending it according to such useful suggestions as they may receive in the course of the argument. Hurtful and wide-spread prejudices, publicly combated, soon begin to have less dominion; the multitude are secured from the tricks of demagogues and the cheats of impostors. To he continued.

THE ALLIES IN CHINA. CAPTURE OF PEKIN AND SACK OF THE PALACE. FLIGHT OF THE EMPEROR. FATE OF THE EUROPEAN CAPTIVES,

We have received, in anticipation of the mail, via Trieste, files of papers from Hong Kong to October 29, and from Calcutta to November 8. We take the following from the Overland China \ Mail of the 29th of October : þÿ The intelligence from the seat of war is of the highest importance. Two of the gates of j Pekin are in our hands. Mr. Harry Parkos I

T' ® Qj I 4 H) C «, and Mr. Loch have been safely returned to us by the Chinese. The army of Senn-ko-lin-sin is still in the field. The Emperor is rumoured to have fled to Tartary. Pekin has submitted to us. The wintering of the whole force either there or at Tien-tain is now resolved on, and we have entered on a new stage of this unhappy quarrel, with its close indefinitely retr<ating into the distance. In our last Overland we mentioned that the Allied Army was in a hostile attitude, seven or eight, miles from Pekin, waiting for the siege guns, and demanding the release of the captives who had been taken. There does not seem to have been any change in the position of matters from the 22nd of September till the 3rd of Oct., wlieu an advance was made in search of the Tartar army, which only resulted in a few pickets of tli e enemy being seen and driven back. On the 6th a further advance resulted in an earthwork near Pekin, where no defence was made, being tak. ti by our troops; aud the Yueng-min-yuen, or summer palace of the Emperor, was taken and completely looted, affording immense spoil. The chief share of the plunder appears to have fallen to the French, who hadthe first, ransacking of the rich ornaments, jewels and clocks and watches, the rich robes aud embroidered silks, of the Son of Heaven; but a quantity of treasure which was taken is to be divided between both French and English. Some privates are said to have sold their shares for about 30,000 francs. The entire British share, including both treasure and pri-

vate loot, is estimated at about $90,000. Next day, in reply to a demand for the release of the prisoners, Messrs. Parkes aud Loch were given up, together with a Fr nch officer and seven or eight privates. Later letters than those we have received bring unfavourable accounts in regard to the other prisoners, but they do not appear to speak with authority, nor do we attach much importance to them. On the 12th everything was prepared for the first great event of the war þÿ the assault or the occupation of Pekin þÿ the unviolated capital of China. The siege guns and other artillery were in a position to bombard the town, unless it should be surrendered by noon of the 13ih. Just immediately before the period given for surrender would expire, Hang-chti came out and said that our demands were acceded to, no resistance would be made, aud the gate was at our disposal. Thereon the outer and inuer gates were immediately taken possession of; and a portion of the Allied force was quartered on the wall of Pekin. What arrangements will now be come to, and with whom the treaty will be made, are matters of conjectuie. It was reported that the Emperor had fled to his Palace of Yehol, in Taitary, that Tartars were threatening our communications with Tien-tain, and that Sir Hope Grant intended, in any circumstances, to return toTien-tain in a fortnight, in order to make preparations for wintering there. There is nothing unlikely about these reports, and should they turn out to be correct,

the expedition will not only have to winter in the north, but may have to take new fortifications, to enter ou new campaigns, aud to be involved in new diplomatic difficulties. The Earl of Elgin and Baron Gros are at the military headquarters; but, as Mr. Bruce has been sent for, it is possible that his lordship docs not propose to spend the winter in the north. Mr. Bruce, however, was sent for before, after the occupation of Tin-tain. Count Ignatief, the Russian Minister, followed the Allies to Tien-tsin, where we believe he is still. Mr. Ward, the American Minister, came down here the other day, on his way home. A letter, dated the 9th of October, from the camp of the British army, says : þÿ In the evening of the 6th a communication was made to the authorities, demanding the release of the prisoners. A promise was given that those who were in the capital should be released next day. The surrender of the gate was also demanded, with an intimation that it would otherwise be taken. The first has happily been complied with bo far that we had the pleasure yesterday of welcoming the return of Messrs. Parkes and Loch, with a French officer attached to the Societe Scientifique, and six or eight French and privates of the Sikh cavalry. They were, whilst with San-ko-lin-sin's army, treated in a most cruel mauner, forced to kneel

before every mandarin, however petty, their faces rubbed in the dust, they were bound with their bands behind them and carried on horses to Tung-chow, and thence, in the same state, in one of the carts of the country, to Pekin, when they were placed in dungeons, and remained so until (en days ago, Mr. Parkes was beaten when he did not instantly reply to a question, and Mr. Loch because he could not speak Chinese. Within the last week these atrocities have been discontinued, and they have met with some consideration. It appears that, when the party was returning from Tungchow, where you will remember Mr. Parkes went to remonstrate against tbe Taitars encamping on the ground appropriated to the British army, they arrived at Chank-kia-wan, where the battle of the 18th was fought and seeing preparations for an attack, they consulted together whether to charge through them or to apply to San-ko-lin-sin, who was a short distance behind, for a pass. They resolved on the latter course. He received them with insult and abuse, and made prisoners of them. They do not know where the rest of the captives are, but suppose them to be with San-ko-lin-sin's army, whether in or out of Pekin is not knowu. Another letter from the camp before Pekin, dated Oct. 13, has the following : þÿ Last evening nine 8owars of the Sikh cavalry were released and came into camp. They bring the distressing news that Captain Anderson and Mr. de Norman died from the effects of the brutal treatment received from the Tartars, the

former on the 8th, the latteronthe 11th day alter they were captured ; the wounds caused by the cords binding their wrists, insufficu nt foodb and other inhuman torture having caused their death. One of these Sikhs, as serjt ant, was. bound with them, he suivived, and has made a deposition of tbe facts, they are all suffering much, and it will be long In fore they can return, to duty. They were brought from a town some 30 or 40 miles off, to which they were conveyed soon alter their capture. No information has been obtained about the two other Europe ans. Captain Brabazon and Mr. Bowlby, the Times special correspondent. The Emperor accedes to all our demands. Harry Parkes and Colonel Stephenson, the Deputy- Adjutant-Genr., went in a hall of reception outside this morning to confer with Hung Key (late Hoppo of Canton). They told him the city would be bombarded if it was not surrendered at noon. The siege guns were in position, and other artillery ready to open fire at the hour appointed, where, at a quarter before 12 o'clock, Hung Key came out and said all our demands were acceded to, the gate was open, and no resistance would be made. The Generals and staff, with the Punjabees and 67th Regiment, then entered the outlier and inner gates, aud asceuded to the ramparts and took possession of the gate and a number of brass guns (thirty I believe), and mounted our guns in their place. The British Jack and the French tri-colour were hoisted, the former on a high pole by the side of the gate, the latter out

of one of the portholes, where they show that Pekin was in the occupation of the Allies, and that the vaunted invincibility of the Imperial celestial city was a myth. The wall is 60 feet wide and paved, and the troops inside have their tents pitched on it. The only thing the Chinese asked was that the Chinese Coolies should not be allowed to enter the city. This was conceded. I wrote to you on the 9th relating that the British army encamped here on the 6th. The French on the same evening attacked the Emperor's Summer Palace, Yuen-min-yuen, entered aud sacked it, while the only British troops present where the cavalry and artillery, who were, by command of the French General, placed in a position to cut off retreating Tartars. There were none, as the Palace was only occupied by 300 eunuchs, and 30 or 40 men in charge of the gardens. They made a slight show of resistance, when two were killed, and

two French officers wounded. The next day the Palace was given up to indiscriminate loot after the French had made first selection. They got a vast amount of jewellery, watches, &c., much of which could be purchased from them alterwards at very low prices. Some privates sold their shares for as muchas30,000f. The officers, from the General downwards, are said to have enriched themselves greatly. A General Older from the British Commander-in-Chief desired that all articles takeu by officers and men were to be sent in for sale by public auction, for the benefit of 'he army, which was done. All were permitted to have the articles they hud brought away for themselves valued, and have the option of taking or rejecting them. Many beautiful curios and souvenirs were thus obtained at a nominal price. The sale realised $32,000, which, with the value of the treasure estimated at $61 .000, is to be divided as prize-money on the spot. The pressure of the people is said to have had great, weight in inducing the autbo|ities to yield. I believe that their yielding now under piessure is the same as at Tien-tain in 1858, and that if we retiie from hence they will again break their engagements. There is no other guarantee for us than keeping the ground we have gained, having beaten the aruiy out of the field. Letters wete found in the Palace from Sanko-lin-stn to the Emperor, assuring him of his confidence in being able to annihilate us by the arrangements he had made on the road atCliang-

kia-wau, where the battle of the 18th ultimo was fought. He begged the Emperor to have no apptehensious as to the results, that having ascertained how few our numbers were, lie was confident he could surround aud destroy us. The garrison of Pckiu is reported to be 60,000 to 70,000 men, or eight standards of S,u00 each; but probably not thiee-lourths of ttiat number exists. T tie re were a few guns on the wall opposite to our battery, and our woiks for riflemen were extcuded to witliiu 190 yards of the wall. Sau-ku-liu-sin, it is said, was in P. kiu this moruiug.

The report of Count Persiguy which precedes this decree contains the following : þÿ " Oblivion of the pa.-t will he a new token tendered by the generous policy of the Emperor, which aims at the reconciliation and union of all the inti lligence of the country. I have invited the press to use great freedom of discussion. But against those who may attack the Slate my conscience will he so much the Irecr and stronger, liecause in effacing the past his Majesty offers to wi iters an opportunity of di-playing their patriotism. 'I he 1'rogres de Lyons announces that among the great projects which occupy the atteiitiou of the Emperor is the purchase by the State of all the French railways. It appeals that this arrangement is to he carried in t o effect in the couise of next year. One of the reasons given to prove that such a plan is inevitable is the inability of some of the railway companies to complete certain secondary lines without reducing the dividends produced by working the gieat lines. In the west centre and south of France many lines exi.-t only on paper, and others have been meiely commenced. The State would engage to complete all the proposed railway lines within a limited period. The rights of the shareholders, great and small, are to be secured by the following arrangement. The average amount of the dividends paid for the last three years would be taken as the value,

and the shareholders will receive an equal aunuity iu Government stock. The rrogres adds that such a plan has been frequently suggested. It is now, however, more seriously entertained, as it is believed that among other good consequences it would put an end to a groat deal of gambliug.
