SPAIN. The Correspondencia of Madrid, of the 7th, gives the following account of the attempted assassination of Marshal O'Donnell, the l)uke of Tetuan : þÿ " Yesterday evening, at 6 o'clock, as the Dttke of Tetuau was leaving the Senate, a bystauder wrapped up in a cloak approached him, and, preseutiug a pistol, fired at him, say- ing, Die traitor I' A shorthand writer pre- ' sent. who was also a physician, at once examined the General's wound, and found that it was very slight. Ou feeling himself wounded, the Duke exclaimed, ' Neither the African balls nor those of Madrid can hurt me I' " When the event became known, the English and French Ministers, aud other members of the diplomatic body, and a great many members of the two Chambers, waited on the Marshal to congratulate him The assassin, alter firing, ran off, crying, "Viva la Reina!'' but was pursued and captured. The author of the attempt against Marshal O'Donnell is the son of a sffiool-master in the province of Leon. Nieto Imaz entered the Central Normal School at Leon as a pupil, in 1838 ; in 1841 he was appoiuted director of the school ; and in 1847, inspector of primary instruction of the province of Murcia. At that period a serious derangement in his mental faculties was perceptible. He pretended to have discovered au electro-magnetic socialist conspiracy against the Queen. Thanks, however, to his patrons, he was retained in his situation, and iu 1854 he was named inspector of instruction in the province of Madrid. He one

day requested to appear before the Chamber, and there be again related his famous discovery, and accused the Government of doing nothing to save the Queen from electric threats. His madness being clearly proved, he was removed from his situation, and during the last six years has had no public employment.

AUSTRIA. A letter from Berlin dated the 7th instant, iu the Hamburg Borscnhalle, says: þÿ " We have received to-day such serious news from Austria, and especially from Hungary, that we hesitate to publish it. In Hungary itself the Germans consider the explosion of an organised revolution simply a question of time, and we are informed that Vcnetia will not be attacked either by land or sea; that the Italians will know how to couquer it in Hungary. At Vienna a common action between the two nations is believed in. We are also informed that, on the fiiat indication of a serious complication, Russia will concentrate a great portion of her disposable army in Poland and on the Hungarian frontier, and that she will take position on the whole frontier line of that country." The disturbances which ocpurred in Nyiregyhaza on tbe 2nd instant were of a very serious nature. The people, who were armed with prongs, axes and clubs, not only smashed many windows and window frames, but burst open the gates and doors of persons distasteful to them. The fury of the mob was directed against the so-called "patental Protestants," that is,agaiust those Slavonic Protestants who accepted tbe Imperial Patent of September, 1859 Several persons were wounded, and many more arrested. There have agaiu been disturbances at Debreczin; andatNagy Koros, at own with 18,000 inhabitants in the county of Pesth, a violent collision between the troops and the people. It appears that a crowd of peasants rushed into the

barracks used by the B'inancc Guard, and took possession of all the guns they found there. The employes in the tax and police offices ran away, and as soon as their backs were turned the double-headed eagles were hauled down. The Jagers were called out, and after a charge had been made with the bayonet all the peasants who were able to do so took to their heels. Several families have altogether removed from Nagy Kords to Pesth. The disturbances in the district of Stainz, which lies to the west of Gratz, are stated to have been more serious than was at first supposed. As soon as the gendarmes were in sight, signals

. were given by some peasants, who appeared to perform outpost duty, to other inhabitants of tbe district, and in a very short time great numbers of men, armed with scythes, prongs, flails and cudgels, were collected on the spot where the goods of certain persons who had refused to pay the new tax on wine were to be sold by auction. It is not known here how the conflict began or how long it lasted ; but intelligence has been received that one gendarme aud one peasant were killed, and several gendarmes and 12 or 15 peasants severely wounded. Two companies of troops of the line are now stationed at Stainz; but it is by uo means certain that the disturbances will not be renewed, as the wine growers are greatly exasperated. When Baron Bruck introduced the tax it was foretold that it would be excessively unpopular, and the correctness of the prediction lias been but too clearly proved. The tax in itself is not very onorous; but the surveillance of tho finance authorities is intolerable. RUSSIA. A letter from Warsaw, in the Breslau Gazette, says : þÿ " On the 29th ult., the anniversary of the Polish revolution, several persons had ordered a funeral service to be performed in the Carmelite church of Warsaw. Everything passed off quietly till the close, when the persons present struck up a hymn in favour of the deliverance of their country and against its oppressors. The officiating clergyman vainly requested the parties to stop, and the organist ceased plaving, but one of the persons present, took bis place and accom-

panied tbe singing. The same parties intended to meet again in the evening, but when tbey reached the church it was closed. They then illuminated the statue of the saint at the church door, aud an immense crowd collected. Tho same hymn was then repeated, some persons kneeling to sing it. The crowd afterwards quietly dispersed, singing as they went, a song of which the burthen was 'Poland is not yet lost!' There was no interference on the part of the police."

THE SIEGE OF GAETA. The following letter has been received from Gaeta, dated the 4th of December: þÿ "The war is becomiug more active, and the siege is entering into a more interesting phase. The Piedmontese were reinforced on Saturday by 3,000 men from Naples, aud tliey are now placing their Cavalli guns in position 1 believe, from information which I have received from Naples, that Gialdini will have 80 of the Cavalli guns. The enemy began to throw shells from one rifled gun on Saturday night. Tbe shells, however, did not come nearer than the glacis. The guns of the fortress returned the fire, and shells were at the same time thrown into Bourg, because it is known that tho Piedmoutcse are quartered there at night. The Piedmontese then advanced to the extreme limits of Bourg and opened a smart fire on our advanced posts, but nobody was hit. The Queen's and the Phillipstad Batteries then threw shells on Bourg, and the Piedmontese ceased firing On Sunday the Piedmontese began to fire on Gaeta from their rifled cannon. Some very large hollow shot passed over our batteries, and one of then fell beyond the Orlandi Tower and wounded four soldiers. We replied with remarkable precision. The night of Sunday passed over without much noise, and each party remained tolerably quiet the entire of yesterday. The princes pass many nights in visiting the batteries. As for the King, his resolution is by no means shaken. Thirty men were sent out from Gaeta last night to burn tbe houses

of Bourg nearest to us, but the Piedmontese were there in force, and received the visitors with a volley of shot. The Neapolitans returned without haviDg accomplished their purpose. It is now becoming indispensable to tbe security of Gaeta to bum Bourg, though tho King hesitates to do so through an exaggerated feeling of compassion for the proprietors of the houses." The special correspondent of the Daily News writes from the Mola di Gaeta on the same day: þÿ ''The fire of the Sardinians has begun. It was on Saturday morning that Cialdini, in order to try Cavalli's new rifled guns, directed the commander of the artillery to open fire at once from the batteries placed at the Cappucini. The result was more successful than could have been expected, for in less than four hours a strong battery the enemy had at the top of MoDto Orlando was quite disabled by the effect

of Cavalli's conical shot. The besieged army had not expected the sadden attack of the Piedmontese, for on the bursting of the first shell þÿ six uiortars were at the same time bombarding Gaeta from the isthmus þÿ both ti oops and citizens ran through the streets like mad people, screaming and howling in the most awful manner. The terror was so gi eat that it was thought necessary to offer shelter to the panic-struck population under the casemates of the ramparts. If such has been the effect of the first trial, what will happen when Cialdini opens fire with 120 pieces? The 10,000 soldiers who are now within the walls of Gaeta may be the stanchest supporters of Francis II.; but I very much doubt if their fidelity and devotion will stand a day or two's bombardment. Abandoned as they are by their officers, dragged right and left, badly fed and badly clothed, it is scarcely to be expectc d they should endure all the harsltips ot'a long siege with that constancy which distinguished the garrison of Gaeta in 1806, when commanded by the gallant German Prince Hes.s of l'hilipstadt. The following is from Gaeta, dated the 8th instant: þÿ "Tho bombardment of Gaeta has recommenced. During the night shells ranched several buildings, and even the hospital. The Queen hurried from oue buttery to another, eucouragiug the soldiers. The King insisted on her withdrawing to the casemates. The fortress of Gaeta energetically returned the fire of the Sardinian batteries.'' It is asserted that England, Fiance, and Rus-
sia have requested the Kiug of .Naples to cease bis fruitless defence.

Pertani to collect money and to have a thousand gallant men (prodi) ready to follow him on the 1st of March. " I have just seen a person arrived from Caprera A Turin letter in the Siecle has the following : þÿ than who has given me some details about Garibaldi. The companied him, and has general has sent away all now the aides-de-camp who ac- with him only his son and daughter, his friend Deideri, and his private secretary, Basso. The mass of letters he receives from all parts of the world is enormous, and some of them contain strange propositions. Dr. Riboli, a distinguished physician of Turin, and a great partisan of phrenology, has written to Garibaldi entreating him to allow his head to be examined, remarking that he believes it to be one of the best organised and the most remarkable known. The son of the Colonel of the Italian Legion at Monte-Video passed some days on a visit with the General, and as the Colonel was an old friend and companion-in-arms of Garibaldi when in a America, every attention was shown the young man. When the moment for departure arrived, the latter seemed quite in despair at the idea of leaving, and on entering a boat which was to convey him to a vessel,

he pulled out a pistol, and before any one could prevent him, discharged it in his breast. Garibaldi, his guest, who, however, expired in a few hours. hearing the report, hurried up, and did all he could No for other reason can be assigned for this rash act than that the young man's enthusiasm for Garibaldi was so great that he could not bear to be separated from liirn."

From The Press and the Public Service ' By a distinguished writer THE LIBERTY OF THE PRESS.
Continued. In countries where unfettered discus- )n is fairly permitted, the people are ery day more easily managed by hon-

St. GiillX Ik Hi (I H esty and good sense. A habit of reasoning penetrates all classes of society. The passions, accustomed to a public struggle, are kept in check. They lose that morbid sensibility which, among nations without liberty and without experience, renders them the sport of every alarm and of every suspicion, at once timid and arrogant, equally despicable in their transports and their subjection. Even in circumstances where discontents are greatest, the signs of uneasiness are not the signs of revolt. The nation relies on those trusty friends whose public character ample knowledge has taught them to respect ; and legal opposition being permitted to every measure, prevents even the idea of illegal resistance. If the general wish of the country he opposed for a time by too powerful a party, it knows that the cttuse is not decided without appeal ; and hence persevering patience becomes one of the most prominent virtues of a free state. Men, convinced they are in the right, console themselves with the reflection that it is the character of error to possess but a transitory existence when exposed, while truth is indestructible, and needs only to he generally known that it may prevail. The main difference between a despotic and an undespotic Government is, that in the latter some faculty of effectual resistance is purposely left to the people. It was the right of remonstrance which so long preserved the liberties of Geneva, and it has done more than everything else put together to maintain our own.

The Press is infinitely more serviceable to the reputation of public men injurious to them. It is their security against malignant representations and calumnies. It is not possible, where it is free, to attribute to them false dis courses, nor to hide t be good they have done, nor to give their conduct an unfair colouring. The liberty of the Press is also the surest guard of a private good name. Where there exists no safe means of communicating with the public, every one is exposed to the secret shafts of malignity and envy. The official loses his popularity, the merchant his credit, the humble man his character, without so much as knowing who are his enemies, which way they carry on their attacks, or t he nature of their accusations. But where there exists a free Press, an innocent man may immediately bring the matter into open day. All differences of rank, fortune, and society are equalized. He may crush his adversaries at once by a demand to lay before the public the grounds of their imputations; and falsehood only raises the fame of those it has attacked. The functions of the Press are not always ungracious. To commend just reasoning, felicitous illustration, candour, fairness, modesty, equanimity, is required of it as much as to denounce qualities of an opposite nature. It has as strong a sense of excellence as of error. It is as prone to praise as to blame. Its plaudits result in no imperfect accents of abortive eulogy. They are the permanent record of the lusty

huzzas of a great people. It represents things much as they are þÿ a faithful mirror. Vice, indeed, in all its meanness and deformity, but good its sanctity, in honour in its spotlessness. Cheering as the liberty of the Press is to good men, they who suppose that it is no restraint on bad ones, and no ing impediment to had measures, and of the case. Ministers know noth- magis-

trates have in reality little punishment to fear, and few difficulties to contend with, beyond the censure of the Press, the spirit of inquiry it excites among the people, and the knowledge that wherever there is an abuse there will be a clamour. Thisconstitutes, indeed, practical self-government, which is the only righteous government, the government which the Almighty has left to His creatures. Whoever fairly considers the present condition of England, and compares it with the past, will understand how great and good a thing the liberty of the Press has been. The noble thoughts and writings of free men have infinitely advanced the science of government. Much that was dark to the greatest of the dead is made clear to us by the light of the many intellects which are now, by God's blessing, permitted to cheer each other, and to co operate for good ends. No fanatic primate could now roast heretics in Smithfield ; no judge could sentence a witch to he drowned ; no king could conjure gold into his treasury with the teeth of a Jew ; no blacksmith could count upon public sympathy if he knocked down the tax-gatherer. Thoughts never die. If the Press lie only really free in one country, its healthy influence must he felt in all. Hence, the public opinion which is now beginning to govern the earth. The subtle influence which is felt from Pekin to St. Petersburg, from Washington to Siam. No post office regulations, no clipping out of heterodox passages, can exlinguish the electric spark of a new idea.

Eve could as easily have forgotten the shame of Iter nakedness, as men c:»n go back to their ignorance who have once tasted also the fruit of that immortal knowledge-tree which grew in Paradise. We cannot now be made less capable, less thirsty after knowledge. We cannot grow again as uninformed as we were. No vicissitude in the world's affairs, short ofthe complete extinction of mankind, can henceforth ever restore the empire ofthe world to ignorance. Although Ihe winged words of thought may he seen only by a policeman in his closet, yet will they sink into his mind, and come forth again in some form or other at the appointed season. The Freedom of the Press, therefore,, in any country should he anxiously and conscientiously preserved as a blessing to the whole world. It should not be used as a means of meddling with the affairs of foreign states : hut only as » means of disseminating those sound general principles on which depend the happiness and prosperity of all. Its part towards foreign governments is neither to reprove nor to lecture them. Example in such cases is better than precept. But it must not be overlooked that our Press speaks in English to English people. Foreign governments, if they can, may deprive their subjects ofthe power of reading; hut they must not deprive Englishmen ofthe power of instructing themselves. If our Press is objectionable to any government, the remedy is in their own hands. They may refuse to allow English publications to enter their country. They may pre-

vent their people from learning English. They may refuse to grant passports for England. But we cannot consent to sit in darkness, for fear our lights should frighten strangers, who have no businies to be looking at them. To be continued.

CHRISTIAN STED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 11th JANUARY, 1861. Our neighbours in St. Thomas seem to have arrived at the conviction that man was not created for the pursuit of business alone, and that the human mind clogs without the application of the oil of recreation to the machinery. The St. Thomas Times conveys the gratifying intelligence that, eighteen thousand dollars have ulrcady been subscribed towards the erection of a Theatre. . We congratulate our neighbours on having made so good a beginning ; however, and wo from the contemplation of this very heartily wish them success. We turn, laudable undertaking, to a subject of yet more significance. Our neighbours iutend holding a l'unuc meeting ! ! Ye Gods ! Who would have thought that the people in any of these Danish coloniescould arrive at so much unity, as to come together, in a loyal and constitutional manner, þÿ to bring to the knowledge of þÿGovernment the public opinion on any matter! Yet so it is. A request has been made by four gentlemen in the Island, that their fellow-citizens would attend a public meeting, for the purpose of devising the proper means to bring to the knowledge of Government the fiublic ishment of the Militia Corps, in that Island. opinion about a contemplated re-estab- This is a step in the right direction. It such a step were taken ou all questions affecting the publio welfare, it could not of be all we certainly must approve said of us, that Government measures, since we never complain. This is the opinion, we have been told, which is held of us

by those in authority in the mother-country, through representations (or misrepresentations j from intetested persons in these Islands. Ex- Governor Schi.egel charges us with want ot unity. The home-government thinks us unfit for self government. And yet we take no steps to prove the contrary. It cannot be possible that the spread of the desire lor the enjoyment of liberal institutions, so general in the world, should not extend to us 'T'.s time it should. And although the re-establishment of a Militia, unpopular as it is, is not the greatest ot the many questions which call for the expression ot public opinion, yet we are glad to see that the public can adopt an opiniou ou a subject, however unimportant it may bo; and, wc tiust, that, this public meeting will not be the last of its kiud.

( From the St. Thomas Times, January 5, 1861.) Through the very land able undertaking of K. Schutt, Esquire, of the firm of Messrs. Scbon, Willink&Co., we hive once again the prospect, may we not say the certainty, of having a Theatre soon erected in this city. The prospectus, which has been circulating among our inhabitants during the last few days, has everywhere met with the most ready encouragement, and at the time we last saw the share list, eighteen thousand dollars had been subscribed. The amount required, however, in order to effect the entire plans suggested þÿ which, we are told, embrace a wing for an Athenaeum, a Billiard Saloon, and other additions calculated to give the Theatre value when not used for Theatricals þÿ is thirty-

s Tf þÿ C B 0 || X A V f $ six thousand dollars. But, as the project meets i with very warm support everywhere, and especially in influential places, we see nothing to retard its consummation. A Theatre is a want which this community has long felt, and by some unexplained coincident, as often as attempted has as often failed. But we have said there is more certainty of its being now accomplished than at, any previous time. It will also lie constructed as easily to be adapted for Balls, and other large assemblies. The selection of a site is of much importance, but even on this score we believe there is every flattering hope that a very desirable one will be obtained. Let us say that this is a good beginning to inaugurate 1861, and let us hope that it is the precursor of other good beginnings. There is no doubt that St Thomas stands in need of four important wants, which, whenever realized, will place her far in advance of most West Indian ciiies. We will here recite them, and at same time say that we are in fair prospect of immediately having two : 1. A Theatre, to which shall be attached the Athenmum, and such other additions as are calculated to give value to the whole. 2. The city lighted by Gas. 3. A Pier, running the entire front of the business part of the harbour, which, when properly lighted up aud enlivened by a band of music, would serve as ail esplanade for evening promenaders. Its effect in drawing folks to walk out, who would oth, rwi-e sit moping at home, could hardly be esti-

mated. 4 The reclaiming of the Grab-lands, and converting them into Gardens, where thousands of our inhabitants would resort in search of fresh air and recreation. Now, there is little doubt that some persons will term these very extravagant wauts, but every one who will only take a liberal view of them will see that they are wants, whenever obtained, will bring witli them emolument and not loss, whilst for other reasons than their pleasurable uses, are quite indispensable.

Lectuies and museums, choral tragedies and L .uis Quinze ballets, will h ardly succeed in keeping the attention of the Piussian people .Hindi longer from an examination of the political ,-ystem under which tin y live. The country, which is made op of so many provinces, iicqiii, > d at so many d.ffeivnt time-, i- homogeneous at least in its police. Race, litiguagc, it 1 giou may differ between Konigsbeig and AiX-la ( þÿ qi ll lie, but everywhere there is the situ.: p lice, the .-aim: violence and contempt of law on the part of the higher authorities, the same system of inquisition and delation carried on by the subordinates, who hope to merit favour by the quickness of their eyes and the 1 adines- ot tin tr tongues. 1 It Was with good cause that the English people were indignant at the six þÿdays imprisonment of Captain Macdonald some time back, and at the insolent speech ot tier. Mdllcr. That this Was no isolated case due to accident or the Englishman's ignorance of the German language, or his undue energy of demeanour, is lmw apparent, for in a veiy short space of time nearly 400 such outrages have taken place within tin: Piussian t rritory. It was only the fact of the traveller (wing an Englishman that brought this perfectly common occunence to the notice of the world Indeed, we doubt whether we are right in classing so trivial an invasion of justice among the crimes attributed by the Public Pioseentor Sebum ck to t lie body of which the

Ptdiee Director Stieber was a member. Tho revelations of the recent trial have proved that the law of Prussia was constantly and contemptuously violated by Stieber and his subordinates; that from July, 1855, to February, 1856, a period of eight months, 387 illegal arrests and detentions bad been made, the shortest being at least seven days ; that men were kept in prison, and then, after a time, set at liberty, without any charge being made against them ; that, on the other hand, persons undoubtedly guilty had been spared because of their interest with the police or its controllers; that espionage had been organized as completely as in the worst days of Vienna and Milan j that, in short,

$ T « C R 0 fj I A y 0 S , Prussia, the educated and philosophical, was not a whit higher than the Two Sicilies in the character of its administration. We cun well believe what is asserted by a correspondent that one re.-ult of these disclosures has been to silence tho German Press, which was upbraiding The Times for its alleged injustice towards the Prussian Government. This model political machine, which, according to its partisans, acts only for the well-being of society and for the correction of quarrelsome and unmannerly Englishmen, has been publicly charged with a systematic violation of the first laws of tho country year after year, and with investing an upstait official with powers which make each þÿman p s ersonal liberty insecure The effect on the Government has been not less than on tho people, though it has been shown in a different way Where the public was shocked and excited the Government became ennged and frightened. Such an exposure had never before been made through the instrumentality of a Government official. What would become of the State if men in office could with impunity thus denounce their cnlleugu s of another department ? The Ober-Staats-Auwalt Schw.irck natio- I must not he suffered to proceed in li is revelations and denunciations lie must be not only silenced, but reproved and even punished. Accordingly, the trial of Stieber was brought to a sudden close, au acquittal was pronounced, and while the accused retains bis office the imprudent exposer of abuses has been dismis-ed, to

meditate on the danger of being an honest man in Prussia. We observed some time since, when speaking of the foreign policy of Berlin, that, though it was ot te n stated that the spirit, of the Government had undergone a change since the retirement of Biron Mantc-uffel, yet no sufficient evidence of this fact was forthcoming. The tendencies of Prussian title seem too deeply set to be eradicated by the change of a Minister. Although the re may he one or two more liberal uniting Protestants and Cm holies, and þÿ based minds in the direction of affairs, though and R geut may be a man of better seuse the stronger will than the King, yet both at home and abroad the action of the Prussian Govern- | inent seems pretty much what it used to be. Iu this case t ho authorities seem to have been guilty of the most severe measures against the I Press which ci mmeuted adversely on tho trial. In the Rheni.-h provinces, where the people have a good system of law and judicature, where manufactures flourish, and where mankind is not drilled to that uniformity and pedantry which reign on tho banks of tho Spree, the couduct of Stieber, and the evident interference of the Government to save him and its i own credit, have been commented on, but at the cost ol incensing the police, who have seized every new- pa per which has dared to speak freely on the subject. The Government has made up its mind that the polite system shall not he criticized, even though it may be necessary quietly to modify its procedure. This is tlie utmost which can he expected from the pre-

sent advisers of the Regent, The constitutional I laws are lax enough, and yery many startling interferences with private liberty may take place without grossly violating them. To such proceedings the present police directors will probable confine themselves. The scandalous excesses which prevailed under Hiuckelday and Stieber will perhaps be discontinued Men will not be kept three or lour months iu prison and then released without compensation ; they will not, on demanding the protection of a fundamental law, he told that it is þÿ stupid a þÿlaw, all well enough for talkative legislator to pass, but. not to be regarded by the directors of His Majesty's police, But, ptobably, for many years lunger arrests, threats of arrest, domiciliary visits, interference of the police in private litigation, in family disputes, and in the education of children, will go on pretty much as heretofore. The Prussians arc, perhaps, the most politically helpless of all the Germans. Their Government lias been so lung a military monarchy, training them all to habits of obedience in the field, and a bureaucratic monarchy, accustoming them to incessant and minute interference in all their concerns, that they are nnable to break with the past sufficiently to establish a better system. No individual has strength of mind or is independent enough of Government to try any great question with tho authorities, or to invoke before the highest tribunals those laws which underlings perpetually evade.

One proceeding will cause no little indignation in this country. We are told that the Government of Prussia þÿ has commenced a state proþÿ þÿ secutiou against eleven English gentlemen, þÿ Procureur du Roi, and speech þÿ against residents of Bonn, who drew up a protest the scandalous inserted the same in uttered by the þÿ tho local þÿpaper. Now, although, according to international law, an Englishman residing in Prussia must yield obedience to the laws of the land, even though they he unreasonable and severe, yet in this ease we think the accused are entitled to the consideration of the British Government. Those who read the protest in question will remember that it was perfectly barmless in character, and though, perhaps, diverging unnecessarily into other matters, could give no legitimate cause of offence at Berlin. Tho real offence has been the comments of the English Press, which perhaps gave M. Schwarck courage to expose tho misdeeds of which the imprisonment of Captain Macdonald was one of the least. Should the Government persist in this proceeding, it can only be looked upon as a deliberate attempt to enforce on the numerous English on the Continent the same silence respecting what they see and hear as already prevails among the well drilled Prussians.

From þÿ1 The Press and the Public þÿService. By a distinguished writer THE LIBERTY OF THE PRESS.

C ond tided.! It is difficult for a > an of ordinary experience to feel much enthusiasm about the generality of newspapers. The nation owes, indeed, a deep debt ot gratitude to the conductors of the Times. In ti day of great national peril anil humiliation, they formed an honourable hand of gentlemen, who were proof to evety seduction, sneer, anil menace, which could l>e directly or indirectly brought to influence them : to the threats of a censorship, to the imputation ol the worst motives. They fearlessly told on their sad and painful truths, till the great heart ol the nation was stirred to its inmost depths, and the evils discovered Ity their untiring and dauntless energy, by their courage and fortit de, which shrunk from no form of privation or of death, were happily remedied. An idle argument has, however, sometimes been used against the interference of the Press in such matters. The Government, it is said, will not he dictated to by newspapers; any cause or individual censured by them shall he supported ; any cause or individual whose claims are advocated by them shall lind it a disadvantage. Yet, what matters it to wise men whence advice comes, so that it is good advice. Government should never feel that restraint irksome, which only constrains it to he just. Its power is not private property, to he used according to the suggestions of pride or caprice; hut a public trust. The problem Government should seek to solve, therefore, is how to use it rightly for the public weal. too The Times has grown mighty a

power to he influenced by small motives ; it has, therefore, during many years, been the consistent opponent of every abuse, however intrenched and protected, which has been made plain. But it has justly felt that its influence was decisive, and has thoughtfully paused for irrefragable proof. It has seldom, therefore, been in the van of attack, but in the centre; and its great arm has thus smitten down evils so ancient and so vast, that any other arm would have been lifted against them in vain. The Post and one or two other newspapers have also done fair service, on many occasions. But the abominable and contemptible trick of hedging and diplomatizing, which has nonsensically been thought essential to statesmanship, is fast seizing hold of journalism, and there are few papers in Britain that either can or will speak plainly. It is this wretched mixture of weakness and cunning, which has tended so often to lower the influence of newspapers. The reason they do not always flourish, when is sup- that they ported by the requisite ability, truth- are not always honestly and fully conducted. The persons connected with them have often some trumpery private object which they serve to their own loss and disrepute. But it is never difficult to predict that any body of gentlemen, who agree to look at public questions on higher grounds than party grounds, will earn both success and reputation. The public is always gratified to hear the truth, and eagerly supports every respectable literary enter-
prise. There is a small part of the newspaper press, however, quite able to praise itself; and it does so with a downright straightforward eflrontery, sometimes

S T. C 8 0 (I AVIS , amusing, and sometimes contemptible. Scarcely any great author has long remained connected with it. Coleridge tried it, and a fellow whose name is never remembered hut in connection with the great poet, got into an ignoble dispute with him, and has left some coarse abuse of the man of genius. Moore and Scott tried the same experiment, hut the result in every case was discouraging. Between writers of hooks and writers of newspapers, there is often, to the shame of human nature, a great deal of positive jealousy and illfeeling. A man of genius, who would live by the Press, must sell his principles, forget his wisdom, and mar his wit ; for the class of speculators who trade upon principle, wisdom, and wit, are seldom very good judges of the commodity they purchase. There is, therefore, a small portion of the Press which is nothing but a sturdy sham. Verba et Voces. It can be bought like other things. It can he influenced by cajoleries, by jealousies and enmities, by likes and dislikes. It is free from none of the taint which clings to most earthly things. Hence men, by no means illiberal in their general views, have learned to confound the honest with the dishonest, and to look on newspapers with little respect or kindness. The fault, however, does not even here rest so much with the newspapers as their readers. If a newspaper does not express the ideas and sentiments which happen to he in fashion ; if subscribers do not read their own prejudices repeated in decent language, they soon

cease to read it at all. A leader by Strafford or Filmer would disgust the Carlton. An article by Milton or Locke would disturb the temper ofthe reform Club. Everybody agrees to be satisfied with a compromise, no matter how unsatisfactory ; and to stop half-way this their course of good. But when all in is freely admitted, when all is granted that can in any way be urged against it, our free Press is still the most admira- i ble of our institutions. It is really surprising, all things considered, not that there is so much objectionable in it, but that there is so little ; and that newspaper writers are as fair and upright a body of gentlemen as they undoubtedly are. Notwithstanding a great deal of fustian and bad taste, with many other things as little to be commended, a free Press must, in its nature, be an instrument of good. It is as much as can he hoped from any human institution, that the good shall greatly exceed the evil of it. There is nothing quite perfect. It is certain that a free Press, under the least favourable circumstances, is more conducive to the public welfare than a censorship, however disguised, under the best The Press, indeed, has fallen under the very power it has created. It must be the friend of all opinions which can stand the tost of time. It requires, however, all the native vigour of truth to prevail against a popular delusion,; and until a principle is thoroughly established and widely admitted, it can seldom hope for effectual help from

newspapers. It is, perhaps, even better thus. For the great þÿman s work goes on imperceptibly; and his thoughts, filtered through a thousand channels, make their devious way to the troubled sea of human affairs, calming if, purifying it, stemming its fierce tides. One by one,

the eternal truths, which perhaps herald the coming of þÿGod kingdom, s are made known to us. They are turned and twisted to suit the views of this party and of that ; they are opposed, ridiculed, nns-staled, denied; still something of their divinity remains throughout all changes: once admitted into the mind of the people, they can never he expelled ; and, at last, those who saw truth as through a glass darkly, behold it face to face. The long strife is won. That which yesterday seemed hut the vision of some ardent dreamer, shall to-morrow be a fact in our daily lives. The use and the beauty of it shall be felt and recognized by all. lie who was firs! elected to reveal it may have passed away successless ; hut he left the pious legacy to happier heirs ; while his hand stretches out from the tomb, and within it, kindled at no earthly fire, is a torch which cannot be quenched, to light them on their mission.

Atrato arrived here on Saturday morning No news of any great importance is to be found in the London Journals, if we except the very ominous circumstance of the meeting at Warsaw being ended without its proceedings having transpired. Coupled with the assertion that, on the the Austrians have concentrated large forces Mincio, and the warlike preparations of France, there is every appearance of þÿEurope s being on the verge of another war. Francis Joseph has granted a Constitution to Hungary, in tile hope, no doubt, of securing the good will of his Hungarian subjects whenever he thinks fit to enter on a new Italian war.

Yesterday morning a smart shock of Earthquake was felt here. No damage, as far as we have learnt, has occurred; and we hope that our neighbours will have as little to record. Major Lang, in his letter to us on the subject, appears to have experienced the full force of the shock. We quote below his remarks : þÿ Monday morning November 19, 1860, about 5ltrs. 24m. Mean time, or 5hrs. 38tn. Solar time, a smart shock of an Earthquake occurred which lasted about six seconds. To me it appeared to come from the Westward passing to the Eastward. þÿ The strange noise and tremulous motion were simultaneous, and in the same manner ceased. During its passage the heavy furniture quivered and rattled incessantly. The noise of the Earthquake was of a rattling character, not that groaning sullen sound which generally accompanies it. Mrs. Lang who had been up long before was at the time standing at a western window. She distinc tly pronounces the sound coming up Irom the Westward or West North West passing to the East South East. 1 never was sea sick in my lite, but it certainly produced a similar sensation. My clock was not stopped, which it was in the Guadeloupe Earthquake. þÿ This I presume has originated in some of the Mexican volcanos, at a distance ot near 2000 english þÿmiles.

Vienna, puhl. sites the following documents : þÿ Pragmatic The Wiener Zcitung, the officio 1 Gazette of þÿ Impehial Manifesto. þÿ To my Peoples. þÿ WhenI ascended the throne of my ancestors, the monarchy was exposed to violent shocks. After a war extremely painful to my patriotic feelings the imperious want of a stiicter concentration of the governmental power arose in my dominions, as in nearly every strongly agitated country of the European Continent. Public order and the security of the greater number of the peaceable inhabitants of the monarchy required this measure; the excited passions and sad recollections of the past, still so recent, rendered impossible the free movement of elements hut a short time previously so hostile. 1 have desired to take cognisance of the wishes and wants of the several countries of the monarchy, and in consequence I created and convoked my augmented Council of the Empire in virtue of my letters patent of March 5 of this year. In consideration of the propositions which this council has submitted to mo, I lnivc resolved upon bestowing and publishing this day a rescript regulating the political organisation of the monarchy, the rights and situation of the various kingdoms and countries, and at the same time the political representation of the entire monarchy. I have performed my duty as a Sovereign by reconciling in this manner the traditions, wishes, and legitimate pre-

When our þÿ ancestors of glorious memory occupied themselves with establishing in our august House a precise form of succession, it was the immutable order of succession fixed by his Apostolic Majesty the Emperor Charles VI. , on the 19th of April, 1713, and known by the name of i matic þÿSanction, which was accepted by the States of our Several kingdoms and countries. Resting on the unshakable basis of a succession l to the throne fixedly established, and on the rights and liberties of the kingdoms and countries aforesaid made to harmonise with the indivisibility of the several parts composing it, the Austrian monarchy, increased and strengthened nal treaties, lias victoriously surmounted the , State. dangers and attacks that threatened it, thanks to the fidelity, devotedness aud bravery of its peoples. In the interest of our House and of our subjects it is our duty as a Sovereign to maintain the power of the Ausit ian monarchy,

and to give for its security the guarantees of clear and certain laws, aud of one common homogeneous action. These guarantees can only he completely furnished by institutions corresponding to historic rights, to the difference existing between our kingdoms and provinces, and the necessities for their indivisible union. Considering that the elements of the common homogeneous organic institutions have developed and formed themselves through the equality of our subjects before tho law, through the free exercise of our religion guaranteed to every one, through the right to hold office independent

of all to taxation, through the suppression of statute labour, and of the intermediate line of custom-houses within our monarchy ; considering further that by the concentration of the power of the State in every country of the European Continent, the common management of great affairs hast become an indispensable necessity for the security of our monarchy, and the welfare of its provinces, in order to tetnove the differences previously existing hot ween our kingdoms and provinces by means of a participation, suitably adjusted, of our subjects in legislation and administration upon the basis of the Sanction, and in virtue of our authority, we have found it good to decide and ordain that wlint follows shall he a fundamental and irrevocable law of the State for us as will as for our legitimate successors. þÿ 1. The right of giving, changing, and suppressing laws shall only he exercised by us and ottr successors, with the concurrence of the diets lawfully assembled, and of the Council of tho Empire, to which the diets will send a number of members fixed by us. þÿ 2. In future all legislative questions having reference to the rights, duties, and interests common to all our kingdoms and countries, shall he discussed in the Council of the Empire, and by its concurrence shall he decided; to wit, questions relating to currency, coinage, credit, customs, and commerce ; to tho Bank, the administration of the post-offices, telegraphs, aud railways; to the future military enrolment ; to

the institution of new taxation aud the augmentation of existing taxation; the conclusion of fresh loans, conformably to our decree of July 17, 1860 ; the conversion of the existing State debts, and the sale, transformation or mortgage of the immoveable property of the State þÿ these questions can only he settled by and with the conseut of the Council of State. Lastly, the settlement of tho budget of expenses for the year ensuing, the regulation of the accounts, and results of the annual expenditure will have to he made with the co-operation of the council.

From the London Times, Nov. 2, 1860. We are now, without doubt, at the last scene of the Neapolitan campaign. Unless some unforeseen event change the fortunes of the war, a few days must suffice to dtive the Buuibon Sovereign from that little corner of bis kingdom which still belongs to him. The great lesson read by an indignant nation to kings and priests and wicked counsellors and knavish functionaries is now almost completed The last days ol I860 will see Victor Emmanuel assume the prerogatives, and perhaps the name, ol King of Italy, with a territory sti etching without a break from the Alps, to Sicily, containing twenty-two millions of souls, po.-st ssing an army of two hundred thousand men, and forming a Power to which the title of iirst-rate cannot he long denied. According to the political code which is uow dominant in Europe, Victor Emmanuel is now King of the Two Sicilies. The voting throughout Southern Italy is completed, and the people have transferred their allegiance by a majority which almost amounts to unanimity There is nothing for him to do hut to take possession of the t In one to which lie has been called. A million of Neapolitans and Sicilians have declared that they accept him a a deliverer, that they approve his acts and those of his forerunner, Garibaldi, and that they desire to belong to the monarchy which includes the great historic cities of Milan and Genoa, Bologna and Florence. Our opinions on the value of universal suffrage as a test of adhesion to accomplished facts are well known, and we

shall not so far forego those opinions as to sing a Te Deum on the success which liberty has obtained in the Neapolitan ballot-boxes. Who knows hut that in some region of Europe the same machinery may be used, as it was u-ed a year ago, to cover usurpations against which all the heart and mind of the country protest? The voting in Naples, however, was evidently more sincere. Of course, there was coercion, inasmuch as the anti-Bourbon crowd hooted and roughly used all who ventured to the poll with a þÿ þÿNo. We are also perfectly prepared to hear that the officials of the new' Government and all those who hope for anything from it used their whole power to make the minority as insignificant as possible. All this is in the nature of the coarse and clumsy electoral machinery employed. But, if we are obliged to accept the voice of universal suffrage when it is against us, we have at least the right to rejoice iu the result when it is favourable to us, and the voting in the Tao Sicilies has been favourable to a degree which could hardly have been expected. Nothing cuu show the influence of a great man and a great cause, even on a people so backward as the Neapolitans, more happily than this total conversion of the multitude. There cau be uo doubt that six months ago a majority of the population cared nothing about a constitution, aud would, in their inert way, have stood by the King. I lie late Ferdinand sent his Ministers lo the dungeon, and tortured men, women, and youths iu a manner

unknown in Christendom lor centuries ; and yet, though all Europe was liugiug with his misdeeds þÿ though Euglaud and France had condemned his conduct by a solemn diplomatic act though there was reason to believe that an insurrection would not want countenance or even assistance from abroad, the tyrant kept his power in peace to the lust, uttd went to his place smitten only was by unable the war of 1809 the. baud of Goi>. Even to move the sluggish pool of Neapolitan life. On y on the invasion of Calabiia did the people awake to the feeling that they were Italians, with rights like those of their tree brethren. Monday the 29th Oct. 1 8(50 the Burgher Council held an ordinary session, as adjourned from the 22d October ; member Elliott absent in consequence of indisposition. The discussion of the letter of Government 20th October concerning letters from the Council was resumed ; the Council agreed on the reply, (as printed in the correspondence subjoined). Government letter, dated the 1st of October, as referred in session 8th October, concerning the offices of the Council, was again considered ; the Council generally agreed to the observations of Government, especially that the duties of chairman and ofseorctary ought not 10 be united þÿ young again, was to resume its full strength, its the present arrangement being merely temporary during absence of Mr. Roihc but declined the to make it obligatory tor the secretary to employ a clerk as substitute (& practically the case), the council considering, that when the duties of the office arc attended to in a satisfactory manner, it is not expedient to interfere about the clerk or clerks employed at the expense of the secretary.

Home, Oct 23. play Hope is hard to kill, and nowhere does breasts more persistent vitality than in the it disof the Papal Government and its adherents. Warsaw is at present the beacon whose rays of cheering light make the countenances of the Pontificals to shine. 1 cannot tell you all the good things that are expected þÿ the meeting in the Polish city a meeting which to proceed from ; is here dignified by the name of Congress. Among them, however, is a very decided move to be made by Austria and ltm-sia, the fo. liter of which Powers is to send an army into Italy to cut off Victor Emmanuel and his combined Sardinian and Garibaldian forces, while the Czar is to occupy Hungary and oihor portions ot the Austrian dominions, to insure tranquillity there while Francis Joseph operates i Laly. Such is the idea which it would he vain to endeavour to dislodge from certain clerical heads þÿ such the startling events on the eve ot which we are. It is in vain to represent that Russia has just now quite enough to occupy her at home, and that, however much she may regret the violation of the dynastic principle and the offence offered to the right divine in the person of the King of Naples, she is not likely' to risk an expensive war to sustain it, even it she he in a position to spaie enough troops to do the very extensive garrison duly assigned to her. England we are told, is opposed to Italian unity, which she fears might hereafter end .tiger her naval power in the Mcditerianean. The con-

tingency is certainly a remote one, hut it is useless to urge that or any other argument against a theory which I leant, to my surprise, is also supported by some of the foreign firm diplomuti.-ts in Rome. The conviction seems that English interests arc incompatible with the union of all Italy under one Sovereign, and we are left to draw the rather astonishing inference that England would witness without discomposure an Austrian army replacing Francis II. on the Neapolitan throne. What part Fiance would take in the game does nut seem altogether set- I tled, and probably that is the leasi pleasing part of the picture which sanguine delectation. have sketched for their private Churchmen One can hardly imagine them believing in their own creation, but such, nevertheless, appears to be the case. As to the departure of the Pope from llonte, once considered imminent, and, even quite recently, erroneously announced by a newspaper as certainly close at hand, nobody here now expects it. There have doubtless been moments wlnn it was p... balde, hut it must now he considered as postponed sine die It can be brought about only hy citcuinsiattc, s that shall aggravate the Holy þÿFather not s veiy agreeable position, and increase his discouragement. Several events are now impending calculated to produce this effect þÿ not separately, but by their combination. One of them, although not the most important, will be tbe Neapolitan vote of annexation to Sardinia, which we are now hourly expecting to learn

The departure of the King of Naples from li is dominions would also bo likely to give a shock to the Pontifical mind. But the hopes based on the Warsaw interview are so sanguine that, when it shall appear beyond a doubt that the potentates there to meet have parted without resolving on activo measures in Italy, this will probably fall as the heaviest blow ot all ou the Pope and his advisers and partisans. It is enter- bable, too, that, until the expectations ptotained from Warsaw have been disappointed, Francis II. will linger ou Neapolitan ground, where, according to the latest advices, the Saidinians and Garibaldians have no intention at present of attacking him. Suppose Naples annexed, the ex-King gone, Gueta under the tricolor, and Warsaw visions dissipated, tin þÿPope s prospects would certainly he dreary enough ; but still it may be doubtid whether ho would even then make up his mind to abandon his scanty remaining dominions. Financial exhaustion must, one would think, ultimately diive birr, to it Tito revenue obtainable from the Patrimonio and the Cotnarca would not suffice to pay his civil list of 600,000 scudi. How are the numerous expenses of Government, of ambassadors to foreign Courts, financial obligations of various kinds, &c., to be met ? þÿPeter pence s are rather a frail resource. Would France come to the rescue ? The present uncertain

Thus might be secured objects supposed to he dear to | the Imperial mind. The Pope would become a French bishop, dependent on and salaried by France, and the Prince Imperial would be King of Rome. Pius IX. will never willingly give up his temporal dominion, which he looks upon as a trust, as a possession which he has but a life interest in, and therefore cannot alienate. But were the choice between France and Sardinia, lie might prefer the former, and might see the nece.-sity of acquiescence, though it were under protest, when he found Iris last resources exhausted and himself de facto supplanted ill liis temporal nuthoiiiy hy his present guardian and protector. To this hypothesis rea- It may he objected, and certainly with good son, that hy so acting Napoleon would create discontent in Italy, would make bimselt dangerous enemies, and wouli forfeit some ot the objects he is known to have bad in view, aud which he may be considered to have attained hy coming to the assistance ol the he Italians lias since aud pursued. 1 doubt whether such by the policy of non-intervention a termination of the present embarrassing situation he contemplated as p obable hy the Romans. 1 he prevailing leeling among them seems to he, as far as I can judge, ttiat a litile patience is all

that is needed to rid them of the incubus of priest government. Count þÿCavour rcceut s declarations arc, of couise, well calculated to confirm i lit tn in such a faith If the French Emperor, who lias yielded so much in the right direction, will leu vo events to take their natural course, the remaining subjects of the Holy See may fairly trust that the mere force of circumstances will lead to the emancipation they so ardently desire. It seems impossible that with temporal rulo of the Pontiff should endure the his present narrow limit of dominion and scanty resources, and with a free and constitutional Italy pushed up almost to his gates. It Napoleon has really, as many believe, the welfare and contentment of the Italians at heart, it he be unwilling (no matter for what reason) to do aught against the cause which he long ago, and in a very different capacity, pledged himself to | maintain, þÿCavour lately s spoken words will he Verified, and Rome will become the capital of a united Italy. The recent extension of French occupation, and the re-establishmeut of the Papal authorities in various towns (including Civita Cistellana, which is not within the limits of the þÿI a'rimoni'i) have unquestionably not only given great di-satisfaction, but have shaken confidence in the French Emperor. It is not known, although conjectured, that it is in consequence of the existence of this feeling, and of instructions from

Paris, that General Goyon lias abandoned his intention of occupying Oivieto, where consternation already reigned of the prospect. No les than 600 persons have fled from Viteibo in consequence of the arrival of the French and of a Papal delegate, and from other places the emigration has been proportionately large from the like causes. Persons lately at Viterbo describe the (Ejection of its inhabitants as very great. A couple of hundred Roman gendarmes j liuve beeu sent there, who certainly need , French protection. The cordial and even affectionate relations that were understood to exist between the Pope ami General Lamoriciere just af ter the return of the latter to Rome, are now said to have been considerably chilled in consequence of suggestions hazarded by the General with respect to iudisj pensable reforms in Umbria and the Marches It might be thought hardly worth while to dispute about the measures proper to be adopted iu lost, pioviuces, but you will have gathered from what I have already written that hopes are still cherished of recovering them. It seems expected that his departure from Rome, which is believed to be close at hand, will not be retarded by any very pressing solicitations ou the part of tbe Papal

Government. It is an undoubted fact that be declined to receive Cardinal Antonelli aud Monsignor Berardi, the Uuder Secretary of State, when they respectively called upon him alter his arrival here. good grounds for believing that Senor Mon, by order of bis Government, did speak to the Emperor on the subject of Spanish assistance being granted to the Pope, and with a view to ascertain how far such a step would be acquiesced in by Fiatic''. The Burgher Council has the honor to acknowledge receipt of the letter of Government No 2390, dated 24th September 1860 ; cominunicuting hist the sanction of the minister of finances fur the employment ef $30,000 of the funds of the Landti easury for advances to planters towards payment of laborers in the present fall; and, in the second place, that Government has been directed to inform the Council, that such loans next year cannot be expected to be granted. Observing for the sake of form, that under the ordinance 9th May 1855 21 it is the Council which giants the advances in question subject to t he approval of the Governor þÿ tile Council can m t avoid to seek lor some explanation of the above communication ; partly, because it is difficult to decide, what is to be considered as expedient or inexpedient next year; partly because the injunction cannot well be understood l ut as implying a supposition of something arbitrary or unlair in the measures in question adopted by the Council in the present and former y eat s, and which the Council consistently would feel itself in duty bound to adopt again under equal circumstances. That public or common funds ought not to be applied for meeting the necessities ot individuals, is a principle not contested ; but in those cases, in which tin advances in question have been made in St. Croix eit tier from the Stated easury or from the Landtreasuiy, the

deciding motive bus been this, that a number of estates could not in any other way obtain means to continue their cultivation, and that an interruption of the cultivation would cause great detriment to the whole community and to all legitimate interests, public and private, therewith connected. The currying ou of a cane-estate, by numbers of laborers, requires a continuous outlay, and that very large when compared to the expenses attending other property (or even manufactures, which latter in case of need may discontinue working for a þÿseason) an outlay not much smaller in bad years giving an absolute loss, than in the bast. The proprietors are mostly new, and have to meet instalments on purchase ; the credit indispensable for them must mainly depend on seasons and prospects. In a slave-colony the complement of slaves implies an indisputable security for creditors; but in a free cololy, and especially where, as in St. Croix, every estate forms in some degree a þÿ þÿcommune of settled laborers living exclusively

T . & 8. 0 I A ft V I Su from their employment on the estate, a stoppage of the weekly payments brings about dissolution; eveu a toreed sale has had the effect to cause the removal of the laborers, and to affect the value of the estate for years. The ominous stoppage of the necessary credit will therefore under present circumstances take place much quicker and more certain, than before emancipation ; and the motives, which during that period weie considered to warrant the temporary employment of the funds of the Colony or of the public for the prevention of great evils in a sir. ill community, arc in reality more urgeut now than foimerly. The ordinance 14th May 1823 cfr. tli a preamble), aud the late extension thereof, was intended to meet snch cases, Si tting aside any theorems about mortgage rights ; when those enactments were of no avail in consequence of want of capital to take up such securities, the public lias furnished the funds. But since in the last yeats the case lias precisely been this, (hit the indispensable money-advances and importation if conimeal could not be obtained, even on bureau for six months and protected against concurrence of other bureau-creditors, also in some very good estates; at the same time estates being offered at public vendue both for private mortgageholders and for the State-treasury on the very easiest terms, without an offer hAtg obtained, ltt most foreign sugar-colonies the security for necessary advances has been extended legally much fuitlier, as almost to do away with any

mortgage security ; this is observed met cly to show, that it may lesult from the nature of a sugar-colony, that its very existence requires extraordinary means to get over bad years. It has not been alleged, that the advances granted fnuii the Laudtreasury in any of the last most unpropitious years have in any ease been unnecessary or itnptoper; nor has it been pretended, that yet n score of estates could have been stopped at the same time, without the w. rat consequences to the Bland, such as tiie administration would be utterly unable tu j tetnedy The Burgher Council can therefore not admit even an indirect disapprobation or , m 'Understanding of the acts in question j On the other hand it ceitainly would be proper for the administration to consider, whether those difficulties, which have caused and ag.iiu may cause advances from the Lai.duvasuiy to Le ueces-ary, si metiim s originate Iroui, but in all cases owe their extent and intensity to delects, which it is the business ol the administration to have remedied In the opinion of the Council such is the case, especially as concerns the want of credit now in question. The antiquated mercantile law (colonial) has essentially been maintained ; foreign ves-eis are not any more prohibited, but the Island is prevented from selling its sugars to foreigners, and from receiving their produce in exchange. As long ns the double export duty to foieigu places (and other irregularities of the same tendency) i> maintained, and the

sugars thereby nre forced to Copenhagen, of course planters are effectively prevented from forming connexions, and from obtaining the credit depending thereon, London or New Yotk, and limited to such credit as they may obtain in Copenhagen, which does not stand high as a commercial place. At present there appears to be only two or three merchants, occasionally making advances to planters, under circumstances where no risk or inconvenience is apprehended, but scarcely when a bad crop is in prospect. On the latter supposition the case would stand thus ; planters are not allowed to obtain credit but in Copenhagen, and cannot obtain credit there ; but must anyhow not be kept up by advances tiom the Laudtreasury, however satisfactory the security may be. Where the. first principles of mercantile relations and credit are set aside, there is hard opportunity tor rigorism with regard to the Landtreasuiy advances in question. The Burgher Council intends to renew separately the representations already made to obtaiu reform of the laws affecting these matters ; and has now only to request, that the present communication may be laid before the Minister of finance. Burgher Council, St. Croix, 9th October 1860. (signed) H L. ARNESEN, p. t. Chairman.

In that ancient city which stands like a mo- j nuinent over the ruius of Polish independence have just met the three lineal representatives of the three Sovereigns who ninety years ago commenced the work of extinction and partition which it has been reserved to our own days to see fully consummated. Austria, Prussia, and Russia have met in their second triumvirate, a conjuncture ,of ill omen to the liberties of Euþÿ rope, as when of old it proclaimed wrath þÿ Poland aud to þÿman. Rut. the spoil that they to divided among them has not thriven with them. They meet, not, as of old, to plot the ruin of their neighbours, aud to divide among themselves that which is not their own They meet in terror and dismay þÿ with discontent at the present and sinister forebodings bo- the future.

beneath them A ucw spirit lias arisen in Europe, no longer the frantic spiiit of innovation which burst forth so vehement y in 1793 and 1848 þÿ the easiest antagonist with which an absolute Prince can have to cope, the most suicidal of all manias, which, if it succeeds in overthrowing despotism, is suie to lay a broad foundation for a worse tyranny in its stead. The spirit of the present day is more moderate, more rational, and therefore to those who rest their claims neither on reason nor moderation more truly formidable. The spirit of modern Europe spurns at theocracy, whether in the person of a priest who has made himself into a temporal monarch, like the Pope, or of a temporal monarch who has made himself into the head of a religious sect, like the Czar of Russia. It demands equal rights and equal laws, freedom of commerce, the abolitiou of invidious and exclusive privileges, and a voice for the people in the affairs of the Government under which they live and suffer. These things must sound to the cars of men swathed in the purple and taught to lisp in the accents of absolute dominion and Divine right strange and horrible indeed, and we cauuot wonder that the Sovereigns of Eastern Europe have met together to take counsel how this plague may be stayed and matters retained a little longer in their original þÿhappy state. Rut the Council, if we have becu correctly informed, lias euded in nothing. It has been a solemn display before the eyes Europe of of anger and impotence, of alarm at approaching dauger, and

of feebleness which has no power to avert it. The interview has, if we mistnke not, revealed to each of the triumvirate the secret of his ovfn and of his þÿassociates weakness. But it has done something more. It Inis taught these Emperors and Princes how little real harmony there is iu their views; how little they possess the will, even if they possessed the power, of united action. The solemn hunting which was to conclude the deliberations of these mighty personages lias been adjourned, ostensibly on account of the illness of the Empress Dowager of Russia, but really, we believe, because the terms on which the Emperors met each other were such as to render a protracted intercourse extremely undesirable. They are gone, hack, each to his own home, with litile contentment with themselves or each other, and with, we suspect, the firm conviction that those principles of non-intervention which they so cordially detest are forcibly imposed upon ibein alike by their weakness and their disunion. The Emperor of Russia must be well awaie that he has enough on bis hands in the interior of waters try without plunging into the stormy his coun- of Italian politics. He is standing face to face with a whole servile population, which lie lias taught to know and demand its rights without having devised any means of conceding them. Were he as powerful as the great st of his an- i cestors, he might tremble before the domestic troubles by which lie is surrounded, and which threaten not only the subversion of government,

but the destruction of society itself. The southern half of bis dominions is desolated by the war which the rashness of bis father provoked, bis army is much reduced in numbers, and even those numbers it is difficult to support The credit of the Government is gone, and it is next to impossible for it to borrow even on the most exorbitant terms. Russia can recall her Minister from Turin, can ndvise the Pope to stand

ST & A t / B $ firm, can frame protests on behalf of that martyred saint the King of Naples, but the days when Suwarrow crossed the Alps to reconquer Italy from Napoleon are passed, not to return. Russia cannot spare her army, aud, if she could, has uot the rnouey required to put it in motion. The Czar may pray against, but lie cannot fight agiiust, the new Italian kingdom. Prussia must at length be þÿthoroughly convinced of that of which she ought to have been convinced long ago, þÿ that the arts of a truckling aud ambiguous policy are unsuited to the urgency of i lie present time. She lias tried to p isuade llu-sii and England, the two poles of the political world, that she is entirely in accord with both. Alter the failure of the conference at Warsaw, she has nothing for it but to relapse into that semi-constitutionalism from which for a moment she seemed to wish to emancipate herself. Rut we should imagine that no one has returned from this abortive The pillars on which they believe their power j meeting so utterly discontented as the Emperor immutably based are cracking and tottering 1 of Austria. His feelings and prejudices have becu us much outraged as those of his neighbours, but with him the evil does not stop there. The emancipation of Italy is to him something more than a speculative injury It commenced by robbing him of Lombardy, and it will assuredly not teniiinte without depriving him of Venetia. He h as played the last card in his j baud by the grant of a Constitution to his dis-

contented provinces. The Constitution is scanned in a narrow aud distrustful spirit, and, as far as we can yet judge, has done nothing towards allaying existing diseoutents. His troops are coliecnd in immense masses behiud the forti esses of Venetia; his resources are exhausted by the effort, and yet be due not take the decisive step for which he has made every preparation. He is not sure of the provinces be leaves behind, þÿ he is not confident against the enemy whom lie may have to meet in front. Something is apprehended from Hungary this winter, something the probability of which the Emperor can scarcely admit to himself. If Russia were only able and willing to give the same assistance in case of need us she did iu 1849, þÿ but that is hardly to be thought of. Whatever be the exteut of the reeoDciliation of which so much has been made, it cannot give Russia the means, even it she had the will, for a second crusade against the liberties of Hungary. Then there is the question of finance, or rather the certainty of almost immediate bankruptcy. Nor is this all The Emperor of the French adds a battalion to every regiment, pours his troops into the Romagna, and, while he recalls his Minister from Turin, secretly approves and stimulates the very policy which he disavows. As far as the letter of treaties is concerned, Austria might invade Modeua, Parma, Tuscany, the States of the Church, or Naples, without giving France a cause of war. Hut France has already shown how easy it is to make a þÿ casus þÿbelli when she

wants it, aud it would he a very dangerous confidence which should induce the Emperor to violate the principle of iion-iutervention recently laid down with so much emphasis iu the semiofficial article iu the Constituliond. Resides, the Empeior has recalled to the recollection of Austria that she herself has violated the Treaty of Villafranca by her treatment of Venetia, so that is a sufficient cause of quarrel. To remain in her present position of armed expectation is to Austria fiuancial ruin, aud a sacrifice of all j the prestige which she lias net lost already ; to advance alone is full of danger, and to recedeTs scarcely possible. No wonder that the Emperor sought at Warsaw nil escape from these troubles in the alliance of Russia and Prussia. That hope has also failed him, and he returns home with very little reason to congratulate himself on his journey, on the state of things he left at Warsaw or the stqje of things he finds at Vienna. We cannot pretend to regret these tilings. Could we see in the actions of these great Powers any wish to preserve the balance of power in Europe while respecting the right of every nation to choose its own Government, the case would he different; but we see nothing hut narrow and dynastic opposition, and a policy having for its object the alliance of Princes against peoples, and we cannot regret that such councils should be covered with confusion, aod that such schemes should come to nought.

The prevalence of Northerly winds, since the commencement of the present week, has prevented any communication from this Island to St. Thomas, much to the inconvenience of all engaged in the trade between the Islands. His Excellency Governor Berg was detained front his seat of Government until last evening, when he left in the Schooner Vigilant; but, at the time we write, the Schooner yet remains in sight of the land, llis Excellency this doubt, great inconvenience through suffers, no detention. We trust, however, that the circumstance will serve to impress on the minds of the Authorities the absolute necessity ot steaincommuiiication between the Islands; lor, had any matter of extreme importance occurred in St. Thomas, requiring the immediate presence of the Governor of that very important and commercial Colony, the authorities would again have had to depend ou the generosity of such foreign steamers as may have been present in that port. We cannot too forcibly urge on our Government the necessity of providing against such a contingency ; as great ml important, interests may, at. some future time, be imperiled bv all intercourse between the - amis being so wholly dependent ou so utir, ruble a motive power as the winds.
