We have the first particulars of the hostile landing at þÿl ehlang, a little to the north of the l'eiho, and the account is as dismal as most ol the news that habitually reaches us from China. We have no doubt t hut as France eventually the forces of will and England two such Powers achieve whatever their leaders think fit to enjoin, against tint troops of a nation never formidable, and now at the last gasp of its political existence by its internal wars. Even a speedy destruction oftheTuku forts and ol the I at tar force encamped on the advance, the Allies, is by no means improbable, though we must remember that any attack ol the Taku torts in front, other than shelling at a distance, appeared to be rendered hazardous by the staking ol the river: that the iartars now show themselves with a tar dillerent boldness from any they bad exhibited before their recent successful resistance at the Peiiio ; that Sang-ko-lin-sin had on that occasion under his command soldiers of a very superior discipline ami mettle to any that had previously been encountered; and that the old formidable enemy, the mud, Appears to be as available to retard or embarrass attack as ever. Moreovet. tlieie remains upon our memory the opinion, rife at Canton, which induced the native merchants to offer bets against our success. Slid: a fact may be no warranty for apprehending disaster, but it, is a warning that a strong and perhaps a most unexpected opposition may have to be encountered.

It would be miserable indeed to entertain any set ions doubt of the victory, for another repulse would oblige us to enter upon sacrifices more trying to patience than any which England Inis endured for nearly halt a century Let us sincerely hope, then, for the speedy success, which will be merciful to all, but, let us at the same time consider as they deserve the opening incidents of this inglorious campaign, and, while Sir John Bowring is tranquilly lecturing on the Ballot at Exeter, take a review of the work into which his and Mr. þÿParkes sChinese policy has led us. The wretched landing in the mud and the trials to which our soldiers were exposed are the we grudge but the fortune of war, though waste of their gallant endurance in such miserable adventures. Then we have the pleasant little episode of the French þÿColonel taking s up the very position which, by the plans expressly agreed on by the Generals, he was not to occupy ; and though he was immediately recalled, we have a foretaste of the not too generous kind of emulation we have to cope with in

S; ( . C; i 0 ( l A V Ij S, the vanity and egotism of our coadjutors. As soon as this is digested, we have to look upon the occupation of the Chinese town, and the necessity of sheltering our troops in it, on account of the relentless severity of the stormy weather, though to secure that shelter 30,000 peaceful inhabitants, women with children at the breast and old men among them, had to be driven out of their homes and exposed to all the cruelty of the elements, which it was necessary for the health of the troops that they should be withdrawn from. Very fortunately there were junks at hand to take some of the sufferers to the neighbouring villages. For our own part, with the troops well in hand, and with a due preparation for most probable events, we cannot conceive but that the inhumanity of this proceeding might have been greatly lessened, if not altogether avoided. A little organisation would have packed flit! Chinese, however closely, in one portion of a town large enough to lodge 30,000 people, while the 7000 or more men landed could at least have been sufficiently sheltered in the remaining houses. The usual apprehensions of the Chinese led to the accustomed horrors. They poisoned their women and marriageable daughters its the only protection against violence, and left these trophies of the first occupation of our troops to greet the eyes of the victors. Even a man who had shown himself an especial friend, who had pointed out all the contrivances of a most formidable mine, and saved, probably,

scores of our soldiers from destruction by it, poisoned himself, bis wife and daughters. to escape the worst consequences ot repeated breakings into bis house, and was himself rescued by medical treatment only to find himself an utterly ruined and bereft creature. The þÿ Times correspondent holds back his pen from describing instances ; they are too monotonous in their misery and too many for the uniformity of repetition It appears that the British commanders have a respect for property in the case ol pigs. A man is flogged for making free with one of these tempting animals, though this is hinted at its rather hard, because the French, who make war þÿ on a different sysþÿtem, appropriate the grunters, and no doubt everything else, quite ad libitum. We beg to remark that this furnishes another motive for declining always and persistently any joint action with French forces. The plan separate of attacks and occupations was settled at the beginning in Europe, and ought at any cost to have been persevered in to on the down very easy drag Chinese coast. It is the bearing of a soltlier engaged in hostilities, and tempted by hunger, as well of to the baser conduct as by lust anti greed, bis temporary comrades. The British example, only one of compulsory discipline, is not so likely to tell on the soldiers of Algerine campaigns. We may overlook the selfishness of seizing on a pi.st of honour to the exclusion ol our brave fellows from their natural share of dainfully forgive that to folks military credit. Englishmen can who very dis- think

glory is to be filched as well as fairly won. But we shall not choose to be compromised, even in the eyes of Chinamen, by the barbarities and cruelties ot French warfare, or believe that on a land, in which wc are told by some we are to be the heralds ot a Christian dispensation, we are to begin with the reputation of robbers, ravishers and murderers. We do not wish to see the British Army stigmatised in the error ot the confusion, far less demoralised by accession to the practice. Merely regarding the misery already indicted, we boldly assert that all the promised benefits of the campaign cannot.

cover its crimes, cannot excuse them in the eyes of any honest man. We look with intense and unmitigated disgust on the fact of this invasion. If war caw be conducted on no other plan, if necessity is to be pleaded for such deeds as we are compelled to read of, if such consequences are vindicated by such pleas, it is better to submit to any wrong that does not touch our own lives, the welfare of our own children, tlie sacredness of our own homes, than to share in the guilt of these hostilities. We can sympathise with the hardihood of our soldiers and sailors, in their bearinu up against ignoble difficulties before foes Imin whom they can reap no honour. But we insist that they should be employed in no such contests as these, involving tit the very outset this horrible destruction of innocent beings. It other modes ot attack could have been devised, the blame lies with those who have resorted to the present ones. If the calamities were indeed inevitable in any Chinese war, a responsibility which we would not share for any gain, advantage, or mockery of honour, tests on those who ordered what must lead to them. The Chinese empire already torn in pieces by the savagery ot blasphemous hypocrites, must, we suppose, receive its death-blow from this Anglo-French invasion. If a treaty be made, who will be left to keep it? When we have utterly ruined the last defences of the throne, where are we to look for a government? We may make the Emperor sign what we choose ; and how

long will he be in his place to enforce his own engagements, even if he means to abide by them? The affair is as squalid as the fiitii in which our poor fellows have to advance to their duty. Some brilliant personal traits may relieve the picture when the intelligence by the next mail extends it, but at present we have nothing but the sordid and t he loathsome to dwell upon, a tone which must predominate to the last as surely its in the registers of a fetid Sicilian dungeon. If we have any satisfaction, it is that the details are so graphic. The British i peoplecannot misunderstand them or escape from their natural impression.

We havejbeen favored with a letter from Washington, bearing date the 29th Dec., whiclt contains the following paragraph: þÿ "The condition of the country is indeed sad, every indication being now given that before tho 4th March, our glorious Union will he broken, into at least, two discordant, and probably hostile fragments. From the Weekly Dispatch, December 23, 1860. President Buchanan is placed in the very singular situation of having to repress the sedition which hits been threatening the American Republic in consequence of the election of his j removed successor, the triumphant opponent of his own opinions. In England there is a sort of chivalric courtesy on such occasions A defeated outgoing Premier, especially in a time of national peril, would be looked upon as a very mean traitor, would feel that he had no chance of future toleration, if he did not to the utmost facilitate the action of the incoming chiefly to put d'own the peril It is a great occasion, and in such the most mediocre of our politicians, by sheer obedience to usage, prove themselves fit to be of the inling class in a great community. We may look in vain Ibr any sign of this magnanimity in Mr. Buchanan's Message. He coldly tolls the malcontents that he does not regard the choice of Mr Lincoln as any im- j to mediate threat to their rights. He declares that they are bound by law to remain in the Union þÿ that they have no settled right of disruption. And then he quite as plainly tells them that if they choose to commit this treason, he, at least, does not perceive any legal tneaus of hiudering them, or of punishing an offence , napping the fugitive. Neither Mr. Buchanan which goes to nothing less thau the dissolution of the common wealth. All this is paltry beyond censure. It is a decided preference of faction to country. It is the indulgence of the spite of failure, oral least

the low triumph of preparing evil for a victorious antagonist. There is a mean man in the I place of an illustrious one. Tln re is an opportunity in which vigour and virtue might have won historical renown. All is blank in cause and effect. Perhaps even Mr. Buchanan may be able to estimate the figure he makes by asking what Washington would have done iu his place. Men fit to found or to govern States never rest on technicals. They go back to the great uses of government, the spirit of contracts. They think of consequences and of the needs of the time. They establish a court of equity iu their hearts to temper dry law, or a-sist unwritten inteulions. Mr. Buchanan should have told the South that he would not suffer it to secede; that it was arrogating to itself most unconstitutional and ridiculous powers, attempting as member of a federation to bind the majority by the minority, and that against the express provisions of the compact. Ho should have told the South Carolinians and those inclined to side with them, that till there was some act committed justifying their revolt from the Republic, lie would hold them to their allegiance. Important Discoveries in tub Interior of Ai strai.I a þÿ The news by the present sit Miner from Australia is iu one respect the most important ever received. The problem as to the possibility of crossing the continent f. run south to north has been virtually solved, and no question now remains that a land transit may be opened up available not only for the general purposes of commerce, hut also for telegraphic communication Mr. Stuart, who started from Adelaide about last March on an exploring expedi ion, with two companions and a number of horses, has returned, nfer having crossed the country to a distance of about 1.600 miles from Adelaide, and to within 300 tinlis of t Ho Victoria River. Here he was turned hack by a body of hostile naiives; hut, as lie lias already reached 100 miles further north than the point to which Gregory's expedition in 1866 descended from the Victoria, the continent may he considered, by the joint, results of these surveys, to have been faiily opened tip froin one end to the other. Instead of au arid desert, it is described to be a practicable country throughout. The full details of the observations made were for the pre-ent, however, kept secret, the Parliament of South Australia having voted ,£1,600 to enable Mr. Stuait to start again with a larger and more strongly organised party, and a desire being en tertaiued to prevent the triumph of final success being snatched from him by rival exploreis in the other colonies, who might hastily avail

themselves of all his information Still, enough had been allowed to transpire to give a general idea of the route traversed. Mr. Stuart and his companions suffered terribly from waut, not only of water, but food, and also from an attack of scurvy. The part of the route io which

water was totally absent, however, was only 60 miles. In many paits there was fine grass, besides splendid gum and other trees, including at least four kind of palm. The event had cteated great excitement and rejoicing sit Adelaide, and the general impiessiou was that a number ot new provinces would ultimately be foimed in the territory thus explored, and that meanwhile the track might be made available almost forthwith to facilitate communication with India, and especially the cxpoit trade in horses. In Sweden the system has been abolished ; and the Emperor of the French has opened the way to its abolition, by allowing the subjects of Her Britanni: Majesty to enter and travel through France without this check on the actions of honest men; (for villians are always furnished with regular passports.) In view of so stubborn a fact as this, we think it next to an impossibility that our Government will continue to uphold this system any longer, illicit, hard as it is to be believed, still exists in this and the sister colonies of the DuniJi Crown. While the enlightened nations of Europe arc rendering tho intercourse of their subjects as fee from such useless and unnecessary checks, the subjects of the same Monarch in these Islands, with but a few miles between them, are withheld from the enjoym, nt of the same liberty. Even when travelling to countries where the to expend our money in the purchase of pass- Passport system does not exist, we are a forced port, which is of no wordly use to n« after having got hall a mile on our way. \\'e have heard of many individuals, leaving this Island lor the United States of America, who make it a custom to consign this worthless document to the

deep as soon us they have got out of the harbour. Cau there he any use in maintaining such a system, except for the purpose of extorting money ? We think not ; and as there are other means of taxing the inhabitants of these colonies, we hot, leave most respectfully to call the. attention of our Government to a consideration of the necessity of abolishing the System.

The Star of the West, The controversy between South Carolina ami the Government is now brought to a direct ami decisive issue. 1 lot President must now decide whether reinforcements shall go to Maj. Anderson at Fort Sumter, or whether the Government shall yield to the prohibition of Gov. Pickens and relinquish the attempt. The decision is one which involves great responsibility, as it may determine the fate of the country for years to come. It will undoubtedly be given after full consideration of the grave consequences which it involves; but we þÿ can perceive no room for doubt as to its character. We cannot suppose for a moment that the Government can recognize the right of .South Carolina to forbid access to its forts with reinforcements and supplies, þÿ or that the exercise of any such assumed power can possibly be tolerated Possibly no immediate material injury might result from further .forbearance, as Major Anderson is probably not in need of additional force or provisions. But the Government would be disgraced, and treason would be encouraged, and these would be the most serious practical injuries which any Government could sustain. We presume there will he but one opinion on this subject throughout the Union. If we are to maintain a Government at all, it must be maintained with dignity. Upon this point the Albany Alius and A rgus holds the following language: "If the Star of the West, in conirnbs-ioii of the Government, bus been fired upon at the entrance of Charleston Harbour, by order of the

authorities of the State of South Carolina, and tho communication of the Government with one of its military posts thus forcibly prevented, there is hut one course to pursue. The authority and dignity of the Government must be vindicated at every hazard. The i«sue thus having been made, it must he met, and sustained, if neecssary, by the. whole power of the navy and army. We presume that Lieut. Talbot will bear back to Major Anderson the orders ot the Government, that the Star a) llie It est must be protected in entering the harbor and in landing her reinforcements. From the London Times, January 17. If valour, enterprise, and succors be qualities calculated above all others to command the attention and fix the interest of mankind, nowbeie shall we find them more wonderlully combined than in the astonishing history of the Scandinavian races during the middle ages. The astonishment and terror of Europe multiplied a hundredfold the numbers of those dauntless rovers, the scoutge of every sea and the wasters of every shore, who, issuing from the wild dales and morasses ol the frozen North, spread over the whole coast of Europe the terror of their name and of their arms. In their strength and courage the Greek Emperors of the East raised up for themselves a bulwark which long delayed the downfall of the Empire. In lta y and Sicily they founded kingdom- ; they occupied the Duchy of Not mandy, and by a feat of a ms seldom, if ever, surpassed, they conquered wiih a single battle the warlike and powerful kingdom ot England. They were the firsr colonizers of modern times, and long before the Norman Conquest they had planted Iceland cud Greenland, and frequently visited the con tun lit of North j America. Yet this race of heroes and conquerors has not been able to escape the ordinal y destiny that awaits everything that is human. We know not that there is any proof of indivi dual or national degeneracy. The Scandinavian races are more numerous than of o d, hut > the natural obstacles with which they have had to contend in a barren soil and a forbidding climate, and the exhaus'ion consequent upon

efforts like those of the Swedes in the Thirty Years' War, have rendered their power relatively less, when compared with the rapid growth of the more populous and better situated nations of Europe. A stern necessity has driven England twice during the present century to give to the Crown and people of Denmark j ouly too just a cause of complaint and too honourable a field for the exhibition of fruitless valour, atrd we are therefore more especially bound to he just and generous towards a race whose blood runs in our veins, and whose language and institutions have so materially modified our own. In another column will be found by the hand of a Dane a very clear and dispassionate account of the present state of the quarrel between Denmark and the German Powers, and we must say that it would be difficult to find in a few years and in a few lin< s a history of greater injustice and more uncalled-for interference. There exists, unquestionably, a strong national antipathy betwreu the German and Scandinavian nations. That boundless industry and research by which Germany has thrown so much light on every other subject of human knowledge has been withheld or very scantly bestowed on the illustration of Scandinavian history and antiquities. Profound Germany, which goes to the root of everything else, has been content to waste lier enthusiasm on poems and legends which are, after all, but second-rate translations and imitations from their great Scandinavian originals. But, unhappily, the war is

not confined to tire fields of literature. The Kingdom of Den ma ik is so unfortunate as to possess two German Duchies þÿ Holstein and Lauenhurg þÿ by virtue of which she is a member of the German Confederation. Sire has also Schleswig, a Duchy of her own, in which there is an infusion of German blood It would be well for all the members of this very complicated and very illiberal body if they had been governed with the same equity and moderation as the two Gerntnn fiefs which are annexed to Denmark. In 1848 they received a Constitution of a most liberal þÿcharacter, a C"»-tituiiorr perfectly satisfactory to Denmark, but which they doggedly refused to accept, because, like the Southern States of America, they had made up their rnitnls that nothing would satisfy their just claim but a complete secis-inn and separation. They appealed to arms, but with signal ill success, and it was only by the assistance ol Prussia, at the head of a German army, that Denmark was compelled to make peace. The King subdued his rebellious subjects in the field, and then bestowed upon them again a Constitution, which the German Federation found means to destroy. At present Germany claims, till a new Constitution can be framed, that Holstein should lie invested with an independent veto on all matters, as well of general as of local concern. Denmark very naturally

S T. CROIX AVIS.. refuses to comply with this demand, and is consequently threatened hy Germany with a military occupation, in order to enldice the right of the German subjects of the King of Denmark to he treated, as regards school.-, the use of their own language, and similar matters, in a manner which suits the wishes of the Gorman Confederation. Now, we must say that we cannot view these proceedings without a strong sense not only Had their inju-tico, but. of their inconsistency. of the German inhabitants of llulstein and Schlcswig been the subjects of a German Power, there is no species of tyranny, political, commercial, or ecclesiastical, to which they might not hnvo been subjected with the most perfect impunity. They might have had a police like that ot Prussia, a Concordat like that of Austria, a Monarch like lire Elector of lles-e-Cassd, a Minister like Hassen| Aug, and an united and sentimental Germany would have left them without a sigh to bear their griefs as best they might. Or, had they been a purely German race whose frontier had been invaded in spite of a solemn European Conveuiiou, as is tire southern bank of t lie Lake of Geneva, or a German province absorbed hy a powerful empire, like Al-ace, the Confederation would have told t lie in to support their late in patience, for from them they had nothing to expect But the case of a German people, the subjects of a small Scandinavian Monarchy, which can bring but few troops into the tield, and can offer to tire Federal army an honourable, but

not a protracted resistance, þÿ a people whose grievances are not real, like those of the German nation itself, but of a purely sentimental, genealogical, and etymological character, such a þÿ people is an iiresistible bait fo the practical statesmen who direct the counsels of the Confederation, and in such a cause they become not only valiant, hut absolu ely Quixotic The very Confederation that will not go to war torcauses that would set any other country in Europe in a blaze is willing to shed oceans of blood and spend millions ol treasure for a cau-e for which mi oilier nation in Em ope would think it worth while to stir. While thus seeking to repress the undue ardour ol Pru-sia and of Austria in this holy and antiquarian war, wc cannot help wishing that they had displayed a little of the same indifference to danger seven years ago, rvh n a very small part of the spirit they are now so eager to manifest at the expense of the little Kingdom of Denmark would have saved the frightful war witli Russia and all the incalculable evils that have followed in its train. We are, however, happy to think that in the present instance Denmark is not likely to he let t without vigorous mid sufficient support. Tire principle of non-intervention, which has worked so well in Italy, may very fairly he left to solve the troubles of Denmark. If the German inhabitants of Holstein wish lo try another fall with their lawful Sovereign, no oue that we know of has a right to prevent them, hut there

are at least three Powers in Europe who view it as their especial business to take care that Denmark he not oppressed or overrun under the pretence of protecting the rights of her German subjects. When we consider the highly critical position of tire German Confederation, its utter want of effective organization for the purposes either of peace or war, the daDgers with which it is threatened, its inability to meet them, the bankruptcy of some Governments, aud the unpopularity of others, we confess that we are lost in astonishment that such a time should be selected to waste its energies in an ignoble crusade against a small but courageous kingdom for no object of public policy or national glory. "Bella geri placuit nullos habitura triumphos."

The proceedings which, by a resolution passed, are to be published in the Tideiule , we regret, owing to our news-letter, and the length of the preamble read at the opening of the meeting, prevents our publishing this day. The following remarks front the pen ot Mr. Ruskin, on the duties of employers towards the employed, we commend to the earnest attention of those who do not think it a duty of an employer to protect the interest of those employed, and who seemingly forget the golden rule to do unto others as they would be done by ; þÿ þÿ In his office as governor of the men employed by him, the merchant or manufacturer is invested with a distinctly paternal authority and responsibility. In most cases, a youth entering a commercial establishment is withdrawn althogether from home influence; his master must become his lather, else he has, for practical and constant help, no father at hand ; in all cases the þÿmaster authority, s together with the general tone and atmosphere of his business, and the character of 'the men with whom Ihe youth is compelled in the course of it tojassociate, have more immediate and pressing weight than the home influence, and will usually neutralize it either for good or evil ; so that the only means which the master has of doing justice to the men employed by is him is to ask whether he dealing with such subordi- himself sternly nate as he would with his own son, if compelled by circumstances to take such a position. þÿ Supposing the captain of a frigate saw it right, or were by any chance obliged, couragement to expect Heaven by idleness and | to place his own son in the position of a common sailor; as he would then treat his son. he is hound always to treat every one

of the men under him. So, also, supposing the master of a manufactory saw it right, or were by any chance obliged, to place his own son in the position of an ordinary workman ; as he would then treat his son , he is bound always to treat every one of his men. This is the only effective, true, or practicable Rule which can be given on this point of political economy. þÿ And as the captain of a ship is bound to be tlie last man to leave his ship in case of wreck, and to share his last crust with tlie sailors in case of famine, so the manufacturer, in any commercial crisis or distress, is bound to take tho suffering of it with his men, and even to take more of it for himself than he allows hi men to feel; as a father would in a famine, shipwreck, or battle, sacrifice himself for his þÿson.

A countryman of his, Mr. Moses Thompson, wished to construct a furnace to burn the begasse þÿ the waste cane of a sugar-plantation that is, þÿ and persevering with this object in view, at last succeeded, lie was led to conclude that the great quantities of steam, smoke, and other products which are thrown off when wet fuel first begins to burn, would, as he describes, þÿ consume each þÿother, if sent into a chamber heated to a sufficiently high temperature, and from which the external air should he excluded. The fire is first lighted with dry fuel, and kept up till the brickwork is heated : the doors are then shut, and the wet fuel, crushed c.ine, tan, or dye-stuff, is fed in from an opening at the top, and after awhile the steam, smoke, and gases evolved, pass onwards into the mixing-chamber, and are there entirely consumed. Thk Royal Mail Steamer At rata arrived at St. Thomas on Wednesday with the Mails of the 2nd inst. The news from Europe is of no great importance. The details of the treaty of peace with China are published in the London papers, and will be found below. The aspect of affairs in the United States of America seems to become more complicated day by day. By late arrivals at St. Thomas intelligence from New Orleans, by the way of Havana, has been received to the 5th inst. President Buchanan has refused to recognize the South Carolina

Commissioners, and they have returned to Charleston. At day light on the morning of the 4th inst., a detachment from Mobile captured the Mount Vernon arsenal, at Fort Stodard. Twenty thousand stand of arms, fifteen hundred barrels of gunpowder, and three hundred thousand rounds of cartridges were taken. The President is however determined to collect the revenue at Charleston ; and the Steamer Anacosta has been ordered to join other vessels, to assist the new Collector in the proper discharge of his duties.
A Fisherman named Peter Stridiron was accidentally drowned yesterday. His body was recovered belbre the boat returned to the shore.
From the Weekly Dispatch, December 30, 1860 CHINA. FULL DETAILS OF THE TREATY OF PEACE. SOLEMN INTERMENT OF THE MUR- DERED CAPTIVES. ENTRY OF LORD ELGIN INTO PEKIN.

Bv the arrival of the overland mail we receive intelligence from Hong Kong to November 16; Shanghai, Nov. 8. The following is the summary of the China Mail. This intelligence from the North is of the very highest importance, as the ratifications of the. treaty of Tien-tsin have been exchanged, and a convention has been entered into containing important new stipulations. These were wrung from the Chinese under the threat of sa-king Pekin, and can hardly be said to have been assented to hy them, but tin y offered a new starting point of affairs in Cbina. In our last overland we mentioned that the northern gate of Pekin was in t lie bands of the Allies, having been ceded to them under the llneit of bombatding the city; that Mr. Harry Parkes and Mr. Loch had been safely returned, and that the army of San ko li it -sin was still inthe field. Immediately alter this the remains of the unfoitunate prisoners who had been barbarously murdered by the cruelties inflicted on them by the rude Mongolian troops, were given up. Messrs. Patkes and Loch had met with some ill-treatment, and endured the dread anxiety of being several times ordt r, d out for execution ; but they were comparatively fortunate in the captors into whose bands they tell, and latterly they were well treated in Pekin, under the orders of Prince Kung. Next in comparative good fortune to thein were Captain Biabuzon, R. A , and the Ahbe de Luc, who acre Mtn ply beheaded by orders of a Tat tar General, who was mortally wounded. We d<eply r< grets

to say that Mr Bowlhy, the Times correspondent, Mr. de Norman and Lieut. Anderson met a more horrible fate. Being tied up in the brutal manner in which the Mongols are accustomed to treat their prisoners, and most scantily supplied with food, they gradually sank beneath their sufferings, and finally expired. There is no reason to suppose that the Tartars actually intended to torture them to death, as they aro always iu the habit of so treating even pvisoneis whose lives they wish to preserve ; but such was the fact to all intents and purposes. The French officers who w re murdered were the Abbe de Luc, Colonel Grnndchatnps, Intendi nt Debut and M. Aden. The retribution demanded for these cruel acts was certainly not a whit too severe ; and it is to be regretted that the perpetrators were not secured. As some of these datk deeds had been perpetrated at Yuen ming-yuen, that palace was utterly destroyed, and 300,000 taels, or about <£100,000, was exacted by 8ir Hope Grant for the families of bis murdered countrymen, and as an indemnity to the survivors for the sufferings which they had undergone ; while 200,000 were exacted by the French General for a similar purpose. On the 17th the remains of Messrs. Bowlby, De Norman, and Anderson were buried with great solemnity in the Russian cemetery, outside the walls of Pekin

Ou the 18th the Emperor's Summer Palace was totally destroyed by fire, property to an immense value being thereby destroyed. On the 15th October Sir Hope Grant bad issued a proclamation calling for the payment of the money on account of the prisoners, and the signature of a convention, under the threat of sacking Pekiu. This was responded to by the payment of the money on the 20th, and the signing of the convention on the 24th by Lord Elgin and Piiuee Kung. On the latter day the ratifications ol the treaty of Tien tsin weie all exchanged. The following are the articles of the convention, so far as they have transpired : þÿ " In Art. 1 , the Emperor expresses his regret at the misunderstanding occasioned by t lie affair at Taku. ''Art. 2 revokes the consent given by the Quern to the conditional susp> n.-ii n ol Iter treaty right to place a Minister in permanent residence at Pekiu. Her Majesty resumes the exercise of her lull right to keep a Minister there, or when it suits her. "Ait 3 provides the payment of an indemnity of 8,00(1,000 taels in all ; that is, 4 000,000 more than the sum already granttd by the Treaty of T.eu-tsin. Tien-tsin is to pay half a million by the 30th of November. Canton 333,333 taels, less the advances towards the Shaineeu site, by the same day. The lest is to be paid out of the Customs, one-fifth of the reveuue of which will be taken quarterly until the whole is paid. "Art. 4 opens Tien-tsin to trade. ' Art. 5 removes the interdict on emigration to the British colonit s or elsewhere, and pro-

vides that regulations shall be fixed for the protection of the emigrant. " Art. 6 cedes to the British Crown the portion of Cowloon now held under lease, and makes it pait and parcel of the colony of Hong Kong. " Art. 7 provides for the immediate operation of the treaty ol 1 i ri-tsiu, and this convention of Pekin. " Art. 8 provides for the promulgation of both the above instruments throughout the Empire. "Ait. 9 prui les for the immediate evacuation of Chu-ai, by the British force now garrisoning it The r< st ol our army in China will rcinaiu at 'I ien-tsin, or Taku, or Tung-chow, or Canton, or at all these place.-, as the B.itish Government shall deci<ie." Owing to rumours, conveyed by the Catholic- in Pekin, of intend, d 'reach ly on the part ol tin I'h , inse, Lord Elgiu was accompanied lo the Hall of Ct lvtnonies by a force of about 3,000 men Prince Kung, the Emperor's broiler, no t him at the door of the hall, and took the lower s. at, leaving to his Excellency the seat ol honour. The piinees of the council were present, and it is said that Prince Kung produci d the Kinpcior's venniliun s'gnature, with an impression of the Imperial seal, authorising hint to sign the convention Both Loid Elgin and Prince Kung demeaned themselves towards e-.ch other in a cold, if not even sulky manner, and the refreshment usual ou such occasions weie dispensed with. Tile arrangements following this convention were that the Allies are to fall back from Pekin ; that Tien-tsin is to be garrisoned by 3,000 Eng-

lish and a small Clench force ; that a sufficient force will be kept at the Taku forts ; that a part of the French force will winter at Shanghai ; and, of the English force, one part go home, and another winter at Hong Kong. It is repotted that the 1st Royals, the 87th, the Queen's, the Buffs, and the Mariues will proceed to England Einpernr was at his " Yhehal," in At the time the convention was signed the Taitiry, whither he had been advised to proceed by the w'ailiko Sati-ko-lin-sin. H. II. Loch, Esq., goes to England by this mail, with the ratified treaty and convention ; and will, doubtless, receive a due reward fur all that he has undergone. The Hon Major Anson, member for Lichfield, also goes home, with di-patches from Sir Hope Grant. The Hon. Mr. Bruce and the French Minister, M. de Bourboulon, have left Bhang hai for I ien-tsin. It is rumoured that Mr. Bruce will resume the conduct of affairs, and that Lord Elgin will almost immediately return home, which would be an untoward event.

majority of the above-named Commission, would be entirely against the wish and the interests of the community, this Mi eting has been convened to afford an opportunity to manifest lic opinion on the suljeet, and fo take the pub- proper steps to biingit to the knowledge of Government, so that it may not come to an erroneous conclusion in this respect, or consider the opinion of the majority ol the above-mentioned Commission as prevalent in this community. No, gentlemen, such is not tho case, and we believe uot to be mistaken in saying that not a single voice except that of the majority of the Commission above named lias been heard in favor of the re-cstablishment of the Militia ; and how could it be otherwise, us two of the majority are the only men in this community who remind us, at times, by a display in uniform, of the splendors of a corps defunct tor the last twelve years What h is l»ppened now that, a resuscitation should he or be necesthat we are awaro of! It would be a gross injustice to the population of St. Thomas to call it, otherwise than a very peaceable one, and for the last twelve years, as was required to maintain order ! ! Not a single case has occurred to prove the contrary, and on one occasion when some excitement was created, originating in difficulties among the Roman Catholic congregation, the police force, and the mere display of a part of the military force stationed here, was more than sufficient to appease it. A Militia Corps would consequently liavo
been useless, aud so it was considered twelve yearR ago by Government itself. We refer to

the rising of the slaves in the sister Island, in the days of transition from slavery 10 liberty, when an outbreak heie was also considered probable ! Government never thought ol having recourse to the Militia or calling it out. No, it was entirely avoided and tot gotten ; the authorities appealed to and called on the citizens to enrol as special constables, and the call was cheerfully responded to ; a sufficient, force was raised to patrol town and country, and under the command of our present President, His Excellency Vice Governor II. H. Bt'.lti), order was fully maintained. It has been said the force consisted of only some citizens or inhabitants, who were mounted, and did patrol service in the country ; such, however, is not the casi þÿ the force was very numerous and was on guard in tt wu, and did patrol town and country. The majority has taken also the trouble to go hack as far as 1826, and has recourse to the l'feiffcr Complot, to show that the Militia was uselul ill maintaining order. Ffoiffer was a tirst, lieutenant in the Jmger Corps, as we are informed, and had with others conspired against the life and property of the wealthier inhabitants of the Island, and was moreover implicated in piracrical undertakings. Well, when that criminal was undergoing the extreme penalty of the law on the battery of the fort, the guns of the fort were pointed against the people, and the garrison was drawn up in the barrack yard ready for an emergency, each man provided with twenty

ball cartridges. And where was the Militia? Why þÿ nowhere ! Pfeiffer had many friends among the Corps he belonged to ; an attempt at rescue was feared, and the militia was again avoided and not called out ; and Pfeiffer, instead of being hung on the gallows out of town, was hung on the battery of the fort. Where the utility of the Militia is shown in this case, we are unable to perceive. We repeat that the population of St. Thomas is a very peaceful one, the inhabitants follow their different callings quietly, and as till uow everybody who does work can gain here a livelihood, there is no probability that such a peaceful state of things will not continue. The military force now stationed in the Island, and the police force, are consequently quite sufficient, as they have been during the last twelve, and many years before, to maintain the public peace, the more so as the large amount of shipping constantly in port might furnish us on the shortest notice with a considerable additional force, and should unfortunately extraordinary measures become necessary, we venture to promise to Government that the respectable members of this community will cheerfully give their aid for the maintenance of order. "Well, gentlemen, in all cases where a trustworthy body of armed men might have made itself useful, Government has carefully avoided to call out the Militia, when it existed, and if it has not been of use for maintenance of order in the Island, what could it possibly be good for?

You would undoubtedly answer, "for nothing at all'' þÿ but not so the majority of the Commission. They say that a Militia Corps would afford protection against attacks front abroad; that it is known that a great amount of goods are stored in the warehouses, and large sums of money kept in the Banks þÿ sure enough ; that the disturbed state of some neighbouring IP publics þÿ Venezuela, New Granada and Mexico þÿ might allow lawless bands from such places to go forward in search of booty, and St. Thomas he attacked by them ; that in case of war with other powers, and an attack by such on the Island, the imposing loree of the Militia Corp. would ensure more favorable conditions of surrender. In answer to this we will say, that the inhabitants of the Island can only he protected by the military force stationed in the Island; that attacks fiom lawless bands from countries disturbed by internal revolutions, are out of the question, and nobody who knows anything about the Republics mentioned will think such an eventuality probable. Their inhabitants may quarrel among themselves, hut tlmy take good care not to quarrel even with their next neighbours, much less attack an Island which is hundreds of miles off. The police of the high seas is in the hands of the great maritime powers, and vigorously executed by tlietn, so that there can he now no fear of an attack which was never attempted when these seas swarmed with privateers, and pirates shewed themselves not unfrequently. Nobody
would speak of Mexico who had previously

s T, c 8 o , ii i ft y i, s , looked at the chart and observed the distance | which separates us from that country. The only attack which has hi en made of late on the Danish flag lias been committed by Dominicans off the Island of St. Domingo, and no redress litis been obtained. If we should unfortunately he attacked by a larger power in time of war, and the fortifications and the military not he ; able to keep the enemy off, we would surely not be saved by the Militia. Why even the majority of the Commission does not think that they can be actually of any service in that case, hut that the enemy's commander will probably concede better conditions of capitulation, seeing order of battle. No actual fighting is expected such a formidable force array, d against him in j fiom the Militia, and we think that there would he none, and as far as the impression goes, which it is calculated to make on the t in my, we think less ol it. Military men hold Mtliiia in low estimation, and an enemy would certainly not give it a more favorable consideration ; on the contrary, he might he irritated, finding that the number of the garrison had been swelled by a Militia Corp- ! Futherinorc, if the English or French should attack us and find any of their countrymen iu arms against them among the Militia, they would he exposed to the in- j 1 convenience of being shot." We have shown what the Militia did not, and what it is not able to do, now let us see what it actually did : "After a young man had attained a certain age, or, if of the required age, had been a short,

time in the Island, lie had to drill for six weeks daily ; alter that he joined the Corps, which corps was sometimes called out for Di ill and for Parade on llis Majesty the King's birthday, besides the Militia men had to mount guard alternately at night. Now, this drilling caused men of business to leave it sooner thau wa» convenient lor them or their employers : young men recently arrived exposed themselves at the Drills to fevers and sicknesses, by which we had to deplore many losses since 1852, and we should probably have to mourn many losses by the same causes should Militia he re-established. The worst, however, were the night guards. If nothing else, people who wanted nights rest to be able to attend to their business propcily the next day, were kept on guard, wasting time and doing good to nobody except to one who Stood sentinel for all the others, for which duty, which he generally performed sleeping, he received a small remuneration. But very often worse things were carried od in the guard-room; playing at cards a ended in gambling und supper ended in ilrinking-bousc ; ; taking after that the young men fell often au easy prey into the snares ol fallen women. Many a young titan has been morally and physicially ruined forever in consequence of such night-guards þÿ and what were the advautagt s derived from them for the public ? None whatever ! " We have shewn that Militia has not been of any use and that it is not wanted, neither for the maintenance of order in the Island nor for

its defence against external enemies. We consider the military stationed iu the Island, and the police, sufficient for both purposes, as experience has shown, and as the revenues of the Island are more than sufficient to maintain said forces, we trust that Government, informed of the public opinion, will abandon the idea of a re-establishinent of the Militia. The inhabitants and citizens of this Island will always give their aid for the supptession of disorders if required, hut they would consider it an onerous superfluous chatge and prejudical to the community if Militia was re-esiablisliod. All we want is a Brand Corps, as proposed by the minority of the Commission, or prayed for in a late petition to Government." COMMUNICATED. 1)11,1). In Xittr York, on Sunday, Dec. 16, I860, the Rev. Richard Cox, aged 52 years. Mr. Cox, for 24 year,, had been an active, laborious, and devoted minister of the Protestant Episcopal Church. He was not, however, originally educated for the sacred calling. He was designed for business pursuits. At a very early age, he obtained a situation in Wall slieet, and was ilure schooled for what appeared to be bis cou se of life. Developing business talents of high order, he received offets which opened In fore him biilliant prospects in life. But having been awakened to the importance of religions things he renounced his worldly prospects, 1'or the sake of devoting himself to the ministry of the Gospel. Although arrived at man's estate, lie determined to make a thorough piiparatiou for the woik. With this intent, with cha tact eristic ardor, he fitted himself for College, amidst all the cares and anxieties of a very re-pon-ible business position. Entering Columbia, be graduated in 1833. A full c urse of study followed in the General Theological Seminary. Soon after his ordination iu ls36, he listened to overtures fiom the Domestic Committee of the Board of Missions, and as one of the pioneers to the Southwest, he p oceedi d to Vicksburg, where he laid the foundations of a flourishing church. After a few months' labor he returned North, and accepted the chatge of St. John's church, Troy. To that city he labor, d zealously and successfully for several years. He there formed friend-hips which lasted during life. But

circuuistanci s at length induced him to leave a congregation to which he was sincerely attached, llis next parish was St. Paul's, Woodbury, Conn. His heart, however, was in the city of hist youth, and he did not long hesitate when invited to the rector-hip of Zion church. New Yolk, the church in which he had been baptized, confirmed, had received his first communion, and preached his first sermon. Here in the those his youthful associations, and amid scene of who had known him from hoy Itood, he spent 13 years of his active ministry. But although surround ed by many warm and earnest friends, who stood by htm alike in his joys and in his sorrows, he was induced to leave this parish of his love. try in a milder climate, which he imagined Having an opportunity for exercising his minis- to be better adapted to his declining health, and influenced by the prospect of doing gt eat service to the Church, he resigned the rectorship of Zion, and accepted that of St. John's, St. Croix, West Indies. Hero in a congregation numbering some 1,500 communicants, lie devot ed himself with the must uutiring zeal, until complete physical prostration compelled him to return to his native clinte. But he came borne done, and after a few months of weakness only to languish and die. His earthly work and was suffering, he entered into rest. In his charac-

ter Mr. Cox was ardent almost to a fault, lie was warm in his attachments, and sell-sacrificing in his friendships. He was earnest, diligent, and laborious in his chosen woik not YY lor a he had formed a plan, he hesitated hen moment in stiiving to carry it out, let the effort cost what it might. From the London Times, January J. Anxiety reigns in every Foreign-office in Europe. Every Exchange is conscious of an uneasy influence, and vibrates like lite needle before tt magnetic storm. The political world feels sensitively, for tins day Napoleon 111., Emperor ot the French," will address the Diplomatic Body, and the policy of a great military empire for the coming year may be revealed. If the fear of some nations and the serious concern of all he capable of gratifvitg the vanity of France and of her Emperor, thev have reason to be full v satisfied. No flattery that could be poure.l forth by the lips of foreign Envoys at the throne of French glory equals tli t which speaks in their silence and breaks forth in their reserve. The instant telegram and the quickly despatched messenger are compliments to the power of France more exquisite than could 1 e conveyed by orations or odes. The Emperor would be a poor politician if he did not appreciate the value of this general deference. lie reigns because lie lias gratified the national susceptibilities of Frenchmen, He lias been tilde to destroy or suspend I i be r t v without losing the favour of the multitude, to augment priestly power without alienating the so-called strongminded si ml unprejudiced, to alter the system of public education without calling forth more than a slight murmur from the world of letters, and all because from the first months ot itis installation as President lie engaged the French army in conspicuous deeds of arms, and asserted for the country the rank of

arbiter in the disputes of the Continent. Republican France fought against a Republic; the first chapter in the annals of the Empire was a war against a rival Empire; but whether at Rome, or Athens, or Constantinople, or Sebastopol, in Eombardy, or in Syria, or in China, France has been kept well before the world; her doings tire the chief subject of international news, her history is made, as in the time of Louis XI V. or the First Napoleon, part of the history of every other country, and it may almost be said that the histories of other countries are only known to each other so far its they come in contact with the history of France. Perhaps in the appreciation of this condition of his power is to he found the clue to much of the Emperor's policy. Those who look on

T c ! P r x & y him as only a Monarch anxious for the maintenance of authority, fearful of the examples of successful revolutions, canj not understand his dallying with refu- W w gees who have for years denounced himself, and bis tacit encouragement of j outbreaks led by heroes who are very dangerous examples to the Faubourg St. Antoine. On the other hand, those whose itleal is that of a Prince who sincerely wishes to ground his power on the contentment and harmony of Europe, and who consequently aims at the substitution of independent nations for illcemcnted and artificial States, who is labouring to remove the barriers which impede travel and commerce, and who will restore liberty to Frenchmen when he lias educated them for it by giving them the habits and pursuits which make men sober politicians, are unable to explain the sudden peace with Austria, the ill-will with which the first efforts of the Central Italians were regarded, and the unjustifiable interference of the French j fleet at (facta. Rut those will probably form a more correct judgment , and will be more easily able to divine the future course of events, who refer the Emperor's acts not to despotic instincts or dynastic jealousies, or even military ambition, still less to far-seeing wisdom or wide philanthropy- All these may be mingled more or less in the strange web of bis policy, hut the thread .that runs through it all is. as we conceive, the resolution to keep France ever active and ever dominant in European affairs.

Under any name or a. y disguise French policy will always be one of interference. It may be pity for Turkish Rayahs, reverence for the Holy City, zeal for Catholic missions, sympathy for an oppressed people or a betrayed King, admiration lor a saintly Pontiff or si romantic adventurer, þÿ it may be a war for an idea, or a commercial treaty for solid millions, but France will always seek a pretext for military or political interference. The means may be a threat or a frown, a promise or a caress, hut the Emperor will have a hold on the fears, or the hopes, or the attachments of his neighbours. lie reigns by the gratified pride of his subjects, and bis subjects value above all things such tributes as he has managed to exact from surrounding nations. To do Frenchmen justice, however, they are capable of appreciating their ruler's moral as well as bis military victories. He lias conquered the alliance and somethings like the good will of England. To achieve this he has yielded in many things to our wishes and prejudices, and even condescended to write letters hardly in accordance with his own dignity. Rut he has, at any rate, succeeded. His position at the opening of I8CI with regard to England is hardly less a triumph t It a n his position with regard to Austria or Italy. That Napoleon will persevere in this policy we have little doubt. The time will perhaps come when be can dispense with it. We must all hope that, if the new Empire be destined to flourish, it may take root quickly. May the Empe-

ror soon accumulate laurels enough to make an easy hed ! When he is as firm on his throne as a legitimate Sovereign he will probably be as quiet in bis demeanour. The French, too, may one day become as unaggressive as Germans or Englishmen. Not that they will ever acquire the passiveness of the former, hut they may ha transformed in character by learning the pursuits of the latter. When the House of Bonaparte rules as

securely as the House of Hanover over a second nation of shopkeepers, we shall care no more for the 1st of January than for the opening of our own Parliament. But that time may be far off, and it mav be necessary to-day for the Imperial management to announce a new spectacle. Let us hope that such is not the case, and that the Parisian public will for the present be contented with the complicated drama which is in course of performance. Thereis, indeed, sufficient room for the display of every French energy without seeking new fields or new enemies. In Italy, Syria, and China, French troops are actually engaged, in Africa, it is said, there are expectations of new troubles. France need not seek opportunities; the year 1801 will probably tiring them to her in plenty. The Emperor lias at bis gates the Anc Empire in process of dissolution ortraus formation, while the people of Italy are labouring with more or less of energy to achieve the independence of their country. The Turkish Empire may soon again demand attention ; even the North of Europe is not entirely free from disquiet through the feud which rages between the Danes and Germans. It is to be hoped, therefore, that t lie French Emperor will not add to the existing elements of disquiet by language of menace or warning, which from his lips is the same ss menace. And yet there is a great temptation. To have such power and such opportunities and not to use them will show much self-denial or caution. To-day the Envoys of a dozen

Courts will attend at the Tuileries with the apprehension that they may chance to hear their fate from the mouth of the Potentate who receives them. The affairs of Daly, and in some degree of Austria, are entirely in his hands. He may tell the Nuncio that it is the mission of Fiance everywhere to protect the interests of religion, and that the venerable Head of the Church may depend on his protection, or lie may suggest that the march of events and opinions has made the temporal power of priests an anachronism, and that His Holiness will do well to accept the position of the first Italian Bishop, with the appanage of the Vatican and a garden." " The hopes of Sardinia may be fostered or crushed with equal ease. Should Francis II. still have a Minister at Paris, a word or a look will agitate the councils at Gaeta. Austria is not a vassal nor an obliged friend, and she may prove once more a stubborn foe, hut she can hardly fail to look for some hint as to the events of the year that has begun. Is she to do battle for the last province which she holds on Italian ground, or do the stipulations of Villafranca still hind the conscience of the French Emperor? Even Prussia, though the demonstrations of Germany and Belgium have given new security to the Rhine, cannot be regardless of the schemes of one who is the representative of French ambition. England alone may look on with calmness, certain that, though European troubles may tax her resources and stay her domestic progress, vet her
safety and honour are secure as long as her affairs are directed by a temperate Government supported by a patriotic people.
